If you plan to implement it, spend extra time on the latency model, exploration schedule, and update details.53:T4fd,3D-MoE combines (1) complementarity-guided offline placement, (2) a hardware fast path for residual hotspots, and (3) tiered online remapping.
1) Offline profiling + optimization: collect per-step expert load traces on representative mixed workloads, filter transient step noise, and infer persistent complementarity relations. Then perform a two-stage optimization: group experts whose loads offset over time, and map groups onto nearby NMP cores/tiles to keep weights local while stabilizing group-level load.
2) CMN (Collaborative Memory-Network): complementarity mostly helps at the group level; within-group transient hotspots remain. Since hot expert weights are pinned to a host core, naive helping would cause repeated remote weight fetches. CMN adds a lightweight memory-controller/NoC mechanism: the host loads a hot expert’s weight tile once from local DRAM and streams/broadcasts it to helper cores via a temporary broadcast path created by lightweight NoC reconfiguration (“load once, broadcast to many”), reducing redundant DRAM reads and packet overhead.
3) Tiered online correction: to handle workload drift without frequent global re-optimization, apply frequent low-cost local adjustments and reserve higher-cost reconfigurations for longer-term shifts.54:T54e,The proposed method is D-PAL, Dynamic Position-wise Acceptance Loss. It starts from the exact expected accepted length of a draft block and replaces D-PACE’s confidence proxy q_t(y*_t) with the true overlap signal α_t = Σ_v min(p_t,v, q_t,v) = 1 - TV(p_t, q_t). Differentiating the expected accepted length gives dynamic position weights: early positions receive larger weights because a rejection there truncates the rest of the block. The same derivation yields log acceptance, -log α_t, as the local loss. When the target distribution degenerates to a point mass, this reduces to the D-PACE formulation.

The paper also separates the weighting scheme from the local loss by detaching the weights. This allows D-PAL[X] variants with different local losses. The authors compare log acceptance, forward KL, Rényi divergence of order 1/2, TV, and CE+TV. A useful finding is that log acceptance is not necessarily the best choice despite coming from the derivation: it is not differentiable when draft and target probabilities coincide, and its gradient does not vanish near q=p. KL and Rényi-1/2 have better local behavior near the target distribution. Rényi-1/2 is especially appealing because it bounds the overlap from both sides. The paper also proves a proposition connecting overlap to the argmax proposals used by deployed DFlash-style systems.55:T925,方法上有三层。第一层是 trace-level accounting。作者从 decode iteration 的共享结构出发，把每个有效输出 token 的逻辑字节需求写成两部分：共享的 dense weights 和私有的 KV history。定义 Mw 为一次迭代中需要参与计算的 dense weight footprint，Beff 为该迭代实际产生的有效输出数，KKV 为每个缓存 token 的 key+value 总字节数，L̄token 为按有效输出加权的平均注意历史长度。于是每 token 的逻辑读需求是 Atoken = Mw/Beff + KKV·L̄token；若把每生成一个 token 还要写入一条新的 KV 记录算进去，则读写需求变成 Atoken_rw = Mw/Beff + KKV·(L̄token+1)。这里最关键的不是公式本身，而是共享与私有两类工作被明确分开：batch 只摊薄前者，context 只放大后者。

第二层是把逻辑字节坐标转成可回归的能耗变量。作者把共享权重项写成 q_w = Mw/(10^9·Beff)，把 KV 读写项写成 q_KV = KKV·(L̄token+1)/10^9，再引入 realized time per token，记为 τ，即总 decode 时长除以有效输出 token 数。最终用一个 affine 形式去拟合 token energy，大意是把 q_w、q_KV、τ 以及常数项放进同一个线性响应模型。这样做的含义是：能耗既受“需要搬多少字节”影响，也受“这些工作在硬件上花了多久”影响；单独看 bytes 或单独看 time 都不够。

第三层是把逻辑 accounting 和物理实现联系起来。论文没有停留在符号推导，而是强调 active bytes 是 trace 的 principal account，不等于所有驻留显存，也不等于所有 operator 的全部访问。像 embedding lookup、positional access 这类不在主账本里的访问，需要单独处理。作者再用 HBM 测量去检验这些逻辑坐标与真实物理流量之间的关系，并按模型和硬件分别校准系数。这个设计比直接做黑盒回归更稳，因为变量有明确语义，也更容易解释为什么某些配置下能耗变化来自 batch 摊薄、某些来自 KV 增长、某些来自时间拉长。

从方法取舍看，这篇工作刻意没有把所有系统细节都塞进模型，而是保留一个小而可解释的主干。代价是覆盖面有限；好处是可以作为 dense decode 的一阶近似规律，用来做部署前估算和设计空间分析。56:T83f,The method has three layers.

First, the paper builds a trace-level accounting identity for decode work. In each decode iteration, dense weights are shared across all useful outputs, while each output token attends to its own KV history. Let Mw be the dense-weight footprint in bytes, Beff the realized mean number of useful outputs per iteration, KKV the combined key-value bytes per cached token across layers, and L̄token the useful-token-weighted mean attended history length. Then the logical read demand per useful output token is Atoken = Mw/Beff + KKV·L̄token. If one also accounts for writing one new KV record per generated token, the read-write demand becomes Atoken_rw = Mw/Beff + KKV·(L̄token + 1). The key idea is structural: batch size and context length affect different terms, rather than entering the model as interchangeable scalar knobs.

Second, the authors convert this accounting into regression coordinates for energy. They define q_w = Mw/(10^9·Beff) for shared dense-weight bytes and q_KV = KKV·(L̄token + 1)/10^9 for KV read-write bytes, both in decimal GB, and introduce realized decode time per token, τ, computed from total decode duration divided by useful output tokens. Token energy is then modeled with a common affine form over q_w, q_KV, τ, and a constant term. This is an important design choice: bytes alone are not enough, because the same logical byte demand can be realized with different occupancy, kernel efficiency, communication overhead, and stall behavior.

Third, the paper connects logical accounting to physical memory behavior. Active bytes are explicitly defined as the principal logical account of dense-weight and KV accesses, not all resident memory and not all operator traffic. Embedding and positional accesses sit outside the main account and require separate treatment. The authors then use HBM measurements to test how these logical coordinates map to actual physical traffic, and calibrate coefficients per model and hardware platform. Compared with a pure black-box fit, this gives the model clearer semantics and better diagnostic value.57:T548,The provided full-text excerpt includes the introduction and the main modeling setup, but not the full experimental section, tables, or numerical results. So it would be unsafe to invent exact figures. From the paper’s setup, the experimental program appears to target three questions. First, whether the two active-byte coordinates—shared weight demand and private KV demand—can explain token-energy variation across batch size, context length, and model settings. Second, whether adding realized decode time materially improves fit quality over byte-only models, especially when hardware efficiency and kernel behavior differ. Third, whether the logical active-byte account tracks measured HBM traffic closely enough to justify the physical interpretation.

The most important results are likely trend-level rather than single-number claims: increasing Beff should reduce the shared-weight term Mw/Beff and lower energy per token in short-context regimes; increasing L̄token should linearly raise the KV term and dominate long-context energy; and systems with similar logical byte demand can still differ in energy because τ differs. If the paper reports goodness-of-fit metrics such as R² or MAPE, those are the numbers worth checking, especially broken down by hardware, model, and serving configuration rather than only averaged globally.58:T515,Read this as a systems paper with a clean modeling agenda, not as a benchmark paper. - Start from source-grounded seed prompts.
- At each round, the editor rewrites the prompt conditioned on (i) the target’s latest answer and (ii) the judge’s category-specific severity score plus explanation.
- From round 2 onward, the target is also given feedback on its previous response and instructed to reduce hallucination, creating an adversarial dynamic where the editor adapts to the target’s attempted self-correction.
- A run retains the prompt associated with the highest-severity response.

The evaluation protocol is designed around coding-agent workflows. Each task runs in an isolated sandbox where the agent can inspect and edit files, search Mathlib, run computations, and iterate using Lean feedback. Because an open conjecture may be true or false, each task includes both the original statement and its full logical negation, and the agent may pursue either direction. After submission, the code is checked in a separate evaluation container. Comparator is used to verify that the submission proves either the statement or its negation without altering definitions or introducing unproved assumptions. A task counts as solved only if the proof passes both Lean’s kernel and the independent nanoda checker. This makes formal correctness the sole success criterion and sharply reduces evaluator noise.

To reduce confounding from agent engineering, the paper also introduces Leanimum-agent, a lightweight adaptation of mini-SWE-agent for formal theorem proving. It standardizes instructions, shell access, context handling, and the interaction loop across models. That is an important design choice because many agent benchmarks mix model quality with toolchain differences. Here the benchmark tries to hold the harness fixed so that model comparisons are cleaner.

The key idea is to read benchmark outcomes as evidence about capability preservation, and to combine standard task scores with benchmark-native readouts such as multi-turn role-play behavior, consistency signals, and psychometric-style measurements.

Distillation is deliberately excluded because it changes architecture, supervision, data, and objectives at the same time, making capability preservation hard to attribute to compression itself.

What distinguishes this work from standard compression papers is the level of explanation. Most compression studies answer whether a compressed model remains usable. This one asks which abilities are preserved, which fail first, and whether different compression families reshape the capability profile in systematically different ways.5e:T59f,The evaluation is fairly broad: more than 35 compressed and uncompressed checkpoints, 10 diagnostic benchmarks, over 25,000 questions, 1,785 multi-turn role-playing dialogues, and 13 psychometric scales. The main findings are threefold. First, compression changes the ability profile rather than producing a simple proportional decline across all dimensions. A model can retain acceptable task-level performance while already losing specific underlying abilities. Second, there is a clear stability hierarchy: coarse, surface-level, or template-like abilities are more robust, whereas fine-grained, context-sensitive, socially situated, or multi-constraint abilities degrade more easily. Third, quantization is generally more robust than pruning in preserving abilities, not just benchmark scores. That is consistent with the intuition that reducing numerical precision while keeping the full parameter topology is often less destructive than removing weights or connections outright.

The first layer is execution unification. The authors consolidate eight enterprise-facing agent benchmarks into a single repository with one CLI entry point. The intended unit of evaluation is the underlying LLM rather than a particular agent framework implementation.

The second layer is fine-grained sub-metric routing. Instead of averaging benchmark-level overall scores, the suite maps individual sub-metrics into six EGI dimensions, M1 through M6: task outcome accuracy, tool actioning, planning, retrieval grounding, safety/abstention, and engineering quality. This is meant to fix two common issues: benchmark overalls are internally aggregated in inconsistent ways, and a naive average across benchmarks hides the structure of capability trade-offs. The paper emphasizes that the routing table is declarative and auditable, which is important if the aggregate score is meant to support release decisions.

The third layer is runtime-budgeted evaluation modes. The suite offers quick and deep modes, determined by per-benchmark runtime budgets rather than manually selected tasks. Quick mode targets at most 180 minutes of wall-clock time, while deep mode targets roughly 12 hours. This is a practical design choice for real evaluation pipelines: one mode for frequent regression checks, another for more serious release gating.

Methodologically, this is evaluation systems engineering rather than a new measurement theory. Its usefulness depends on whether the metric routing is sensible and whether the resulting aggregate signal is stable and interpretable.61:T5ae,The main empirical result is a 14-model quick-mode benchmark covering GPT, Claude, and Gemini families, used to show that the unified EGI score exposes capability specialization that is often invisible in any single benchmark's overall score. In other words, a model may be strong at tool use and planning but weaker at abstention or engineering quality, and a flat average can hide that structure.

The provided excerpt does not include the full numeric tables, but several experimental choices are worth noting. First, the suite is not trying to outperform SWE-bench, GAIA, or BFCL on their home axes; it is trying to compose eight benchmarks into six deployment-relevant dimensions. Second, it introduces release-gate semantics, including configurable floors on dimensions such as safety or tool reliability, which is closer to how real deployment decisions are made than a single scalar average. Without that, a unified score can easily become just another opaque number.62:T5d3,TURTLE is a three-agent evolutionary pipeline:
- Task representation: tool-use tasks are encoded as Python programs (environment state, databases, tools, goals). This makes compositional mutation feasible and preserves compatibility with existing harnesses, but introduces risks of format/underspecification artifacts.
- Proposer: implemented via AlphaEvolve, a gradient-free evolutionary search operator. A practical point is that it can leverage strong closed-source LLMs as proposers via API calls, since no gradients/weights are needed.
- Solver: the target model under evaluation; each candidate mutated task is attempted N times to estimate an empirical completion rate.
- Fitness shaping: reward targets “hard but solvable” by pushing completion rates toward ~50%, motivated by maximal variance / maximal discriminative power near 0.5 (akin to learnability sampling).
- Feedback generator: summarizes failure reasons from execution traces plus the ground-truth solution, producing exploitable signals for the proposer’s next mutations.
- Post-filtering: an LLM judge (Gemini 3.6 Flash) removes trivial failures (format mismatches, ambiguous instructions, near-paraphrases), which is crucial to prevent evolution from exploiting loopholes.
- Dataset selection: after a fixed evolution budget, the final set keeps, per parent task, programs with the highest completion-rate variance, aiming for samples that best separate solver behaviors rather than simply maximizing difficulty.63:T432,This is not a pretraining-method paper in the narrow sense, but it is relevant to the pretrain/post-train interface and to the safety of automated training pipelines. 1. 两条评测轨。core track 是作者生成的受控任务，共 7,800 个样本，来自 13 个 task family，按 contrast group 组织。reference track 是 35 个公开测试集，共 32,233 个样本，保留原始评测协议和已知训练重叠信息。前者强调可控诊断，后者强调和既有工作可比。
2. typed decision interface。每个样本都写成 state、typed question、finite option set 的统一形式，模型输出对各选项的概率分布。这样 routing、guardrail、verification、goal checking 等不同角色可以放在同一接口下比较。
3. 七类 decision role。覆盖从 answerability / routing，到 policy guardrail、output verification、agent loop 中的 tool validation / goal checking，再到 reasoning-based classification、record reconciliation、constraint-based matching。作者想表达的是：LLM 系统里“决策”无处不在，而且这些决策共享一套概率输出与阈值控制问题。
4. contrast-group 设计。core track 的关键创新在这里。多数 task family 通过只改一个 pivotal detail 来改变正确答案，同时尽量保持上下文和表面形式不变。这样可以测模型是否真的抓住决定性变量，而不是靠模板、长度、词面线索做猜测。
5. 独立求解器验证。core 样本答案由独立实现的 solver 计算并验证，减少人工标注噪声，也降低 benchmark 本身出错的风险。
6. 评测指标不只看 accuracy。作者同时看 item accuracy、pair accuracy（更一般地说是 contrast-group 全对率）、probability ordering、calibration、selective coverage。这里 pair accuracy 很关键，因为它要求一个对比组里的所有变体都答对，能直接暴露“只会答一半”的脆弱性。

方法上的价值不在模型算法，而在评测协议：它把 decision quality 拆成 correctness、consistency、confidence reliability 三层，而不是混成一个总分。68:T7d1,DecisionPivot is a benchmark and evaluation protocol rather than a new model. Its design has several notable elements.

1. Two-track structure. The core track contains 7,800 generated items from 13 task families, organized into contrast groups for controlled diagnosis. The reference track contains 32,233 items from 35 public test sets, preserving original metrics and available overlap information. The first track gives control; the second gives comparability.
2. Typed decision interface. Every item is represented as a state, a typed question, and a finite option set. Models output a probability distribution over options. This allows routing, guardrails, output verification, and goal checking to be evaluated under a common interface.
3. Seven decision roles. The benchmark spans answerability and routing, policy guardrails, output verification, tool validation or goal checking in agent loops, reasoning-based classification, record reconciliation, and constraint-based search or matching.
4. Contrast-group construction. This is the core methodological contribution. In most generated families, a pivotal detail is changed while surrounding context remains largely fixed. The correct answer changes accordingly. This tests whether the model is sensitive to the actual decision variable rather than exploiting surface patterns.
5. Independent solver verification. Core answers are computed and checked by independently implemented solvers, reducing annotation noise and benchmark errors.
6. Multi-faceted metrics. The evaluation includes item accuracy, pair accuracy or full contrast-group correctness, probability ordering, calibration, and selective coverage. Pair accuracy is especially useful because it requires all members of a contrast group to be correct, exposing brittle behavior that average accuracy can hide.

The main contribution is therefore an evaluation decomposition of decision quality into correctness, consistency under controlled variation, and confidence reliability.69:T62c,The empirical study is fairly broad. The benchmark is used to evaluate 40 decision models and 14 general models, including 11 open general models and 3 API chat models on the core track. Several findings stand out.

1. Similar scores on public reference sets do not imply similar controlled decision behavior. The paper highlights cases such as Perplexity Decider and JEV-27B, which look similar on the reference track but differ substantially in core pair accuracy.
2. Similar item accuracy does not imply similar confidence quality. Kev 27B and JEV-27B reportedly have nearly identical item accuracy but differ in how often they make high-confidence predictions and how often those predictions are correct.
3. Correct probability ordering is not the same as correct decisions. The binary contrast analysis shows that a model may rank options in a roughly sensible way yet still fail to produce the correct argmax consistently.
4. Reasoning settings help on some cases but do not uniformly fix decision failures. This matters because it shows that the problem is not simply solved by adding more chain-of-thought.
5. Freshly sampled cases from the generators are used to test ranking stability, which is a good safeguard against benchmark-specific overfitting.

If reading the full paper, Figure 1, the per-role breakdowns, and the appendix example showing a content-blind rule reaching 73.0% on llmbar are especially informative.6a:T516,Read this paper with a concrete systems question in mind, such as whether you need it for evaluating a router, verifier, or guardrail model.

Start with the introduction. The key point is why item accuracy is inadequate and why confidence reliability deserves separate measurement. That is directly relevant to any component that uses thresholds or defers uncertain cases.

Then read the benchmark construction carefully. Focus on how the core contrast groups are generated, how pivotal variations are annotated, and how independent solvers verify answers. This determines whether the benchmark is genuinely diagnostic rather than just another mixed test collection.

The metrics section is worth close attention. Pair accuracy, probability ordering, calibration, and selective coverage each correspond to different failure modes. Understanding that decomposition is more useful than memorizing which model ranks first.

In the experiments, prioritize Figure 1 and the representative comparisons where reference performance looks similar but core behavior differs, or where item accuracy is similar but confidence behavior diverges. For a quick read, 25 to 35 minutes is enough. If you work on decision heads, verifiers, or routers, the appendix is worth reading for protocol details and overlap notes.6b:T788,The main method is VB-EGE, short for Vector-Borda Empirical-Gap Elimination. The central difficulty is that the target is defined on latent score vectors theta_i, while the learner only observes binary pairwise outcomes on one objective at a time. The paper resolves this by defining, for each objective, a Borda coordinate: the average win probability of a model against all opponents on that objective. Under the Bradley–Terry model, higher latent score implies higher pairwise win probability against every opponent, so the Borda transform preserves the per-objective ordering of latent scores. As a result, strict dominance and the strict Pareto frontier are unchanged under this mapping. The original problem is thus reduced to identifying the Pareto set of K vectors of d Bernoulli means.

Algorithmically, VB-EGE extends empirical-gap elimination from the scalar setting to the vector setting. It maintains an active set and keeps sampling only models whose Pareto status is still uncertain. Once there is enough statistical evidence that one model is strictly dominated by another across all objectives, the dominated model is eliminated. The sampling policy is adaptive: budget is concentrated on the hardest-to-certify dominance relations rather than spread uniformly across all pairs and objectives. A substantial part of the paper is devoted to confidence construction that is valid simultaneously over models, objectives, and rounds, and to translating those confidence intervals into safe elimination rules. The paper also proves delta-correctness and gives an instance-dependent sample complexity upper bound, together with lower-bound discussion. One design choice worth noting is the use of strict Pareto dominance rather than the usual weak Pareto notion. This is motivated both by decision semantics and by the technical need to avoid coordinate-wise ties that would break finite-sample stopping guarantees.6c:T511,The experiments are designed to validate three points. First, on real arena data, the method can recover the frontier with fewer comparisons. Using Arena-Human-Preference-140K and treating code, math, and instruction-following as three objectives, the method identifies three models on the strict Pareto frontier. Second, compared with non-adaptive or simpler allocation strategies, VB-EGE reduces the number of required comparisons at the same confidence level. The savings come from quickly eliminating clearly dominated models and focusing effort on near-frontier cases. Third, synthetic experiments show the expected gap dependence: sample complexity rises when classification gaps shrink, especially for models that are close on some objectives and hard to certify as dominated or non-dominated.

The main value of the experimental section is not one headline number but the structure of the evidence. The paper includes both replay on real preference data and controlled simulations, and it evaluates both correctness and stopping time or comparison count. For practical adoption, the most useful details are how the method scales with the number of models K, the number of objectives d, and the frontier gaps, and how much it improves over uniform or round-robin baselines in those regimes.6d:T4f6,The paper introduces BenchDoor, a family of backdoor attacks organized around benchmark incentives. The threat model varies along two axes: what data the adversary controls, and how the developer uses benchmark-related data during training. This yields five attack scenarios, including manipulation of benchmark training data, manipulation of benchmark test data followed by rewritten training examples, and attacks where the benchmark itself is untouched but the adversary releases an independent dataset advertised as improving benchmark performance.

The methodological point is not a new model architecture but a dual-objective poisoning strategy. The poisoned data must simultaneously improve benchmark performance and preserve high attack success on triggered inputs. The paper also evaluates two realistic defenses or workflow steps: first, rewriting benchmark test examples into synthetic training data to avoid exact overlap; second, applying similarity-based decontamination to remove near-duplicates. The claim is that BenchDoor can survive both steps while still delivering benchmark gains. That makes the setup more realistic than classic poisoning papers, because many modern LLM pipelines already use rewriting, synthetic expansion, and overlap filtering.6e:T45a,The evaluation spans three task types: multiple-choice QA, text classification, and open-ended QA. The benchmarks include MMLU, TweetEval, and FalseReject, and the model families are Qwen and Gemma. In total, the paper reports 30 combinations of task, model family, and attack scenario. Across all 30 settings, BenchDoor achieves positive benchmark gains. Held-out attack success rates range from 82.33% to 100.00% with poisoning rates between 2% and 10%.

A particularly important result is robustness to common sanitization steps. After synthetic data generation and subsequent similarity-based decontamination, attack success remains at least 90.33% in the reported experiments. These numbers suggest two practical lessons. First, the attack does not require large poisoning fractions. Second, overlap-based or similarity-based decontamination is not enough when the malicious signal survives semantic rewriting. For foundation-model teams, the most concerning point is that the benchmark itself does not need to be compromised; an external benchmark-targeted training dataset can be enough to carry the attack.6f:T573,The paper defines a reasoning graph as a DAG G=(V,E) with explicit semantics. Each node is a triple (sub-question q_i, intermediate answer a_i, evidence identifiers E_i). Each directed edge e_{ij} means step j requires the answer from step i—an immediate dependency. This enables principled checks for shortcut edges and clarifies that the graph encodes data-flow, not generation order.

It then runs a two-stage evaluation.
- Stage 1 (graph reliability): evaluates graph construction under progressively weaker gold scaffolding to isolate capabilities: decomposing the question into steps, wiring correct dependencies, producing correct node answers, and grounding each step in evidence. The design goal is to attribute failures to specific axes rather than to an undifferentiated “graph quality” score.
- Stage 2 (downstream uncertainty estimation): compares multiple ways of using graphs—graph-free baselines, graph-as-prompt context, verbalized confidence, and graph-as-computation. A key stress test replaces gold edges with generated edges to measure how upstream structural errors propagate into confidence quality and final performance.

The methodological choice is conservative: instead of claiming graphs improve reasoning, it tests whether the produced artifact satisfies its declared semantics and whether those semantics are strong enough to support downstream computation.70:T44f,From the provided full-text excerpt, the paper’s experimental takeaways are clear but many numeric details (model sizes, exact scores, dataset counts per setting) are not present, so only design-level and qualitative conclusions can be stated safely:
- Setting: open-ended multi-hop QA with gold scaffolding to enable controlled comparisons of nodes/edges/evidence.
- Stage 1: frontier models can produce high-quality graphs with sufficient prompting, but reliability is not stable; it varies by model family, graph topology (notably merge structures), and prompt schema, and smaller models degrade substantially.
- Stage 2: graph-as-prompt provides limited benefit; verbalized confidence is often weakly discriminative. Graph-as-computation can yield more useful confidence and node-level diagnostics, but its advantage depends on graph quality; swapping gold edges for generated edges reduces downstream performance relative to the gold-graph condition, evidencing error propagation.
For exact numbers and ablations, consult the experiment tables/appendix in the paper (not included in the excerpt).71:T42a,The method separates confidence into two prompted signals. FOK, or Feeling-of-Knowing, is an anticipatory confidence estimate elicited before the model attempts the problem. Because the study includes closed-source API models, the confidence signal is based on verbal self-assessment rather than token-level probabilities.

This design separates surface language transfer from gaps in parametric knowledge coverage.72:T45a,The evaluation is built around cross-episode, counterfactual-style pairing.
- Episode 1 (p_i): run the untrusted model U on a sabotage task under DtT; keep only trajectories that actually trigger replacement (IaC: suspicion ≥ 5/10; SHADE: ≥ 50/100), ensuring the history contains a concrete ‘caught’ event.
- Episode 2 (p_j): start a fresh environment and new conversation for a different task, but prepend the full replay of the caught p_i trajectory plus one feedback message.
- Feedback variants: (1) told replaced (explicitly states the submission was replaced), (2) shown replacement (also includes the trusted model T’s replacement output).
- Crucially, each history-conditioned run on p_j is paired with a memoryless run on the identical p_j by the same model, holding the successor task fixed.
- History-format ablation: full history (tool interactions included; reasoning removed; long tool outputs elided) vs condensed history (only prior task, final message, and resulting diff/actions). This is meant to separate ‘behavioral updating’ from ‘context-length / information-load’ effects.73:T7f2,UniWALM is a unified World-Action-Language Model built on a mixture-of-transformers backbone. Video, action, and language are all inputs, and each modality has its own diffusion head on top of the shared backbone. The key design choice is synchronous co-denoising: the model predicts all three modalities in the same denoising pass. This forces the shared representation to support three different predictive views at once: video gives local spatiotemporal dynamics, action gives control supervision, and language gives higher-level task and state supervision over longer horizons.

The language stream emits two kinds of text: a subtask description and a textual memory of what has happened so far. These outputs are fed back as part of the prompt at the next control step, forming a closed language-as-memory loop. This differs from chain-of-thought style VLAs, where intermediate text is often generated autoregressively before action and is not necessarily reused across steps. Here, language and action are produced together inside one generative process, which reduces the planner-policy split.

A second technical component is Flow Matching with Correction (FMC). During training, the method perturbs action trajectories and supervises a corrective velocity field that steers the perturbed denoising path back toward the clean trajectory. The point is to train recovery behavior in action generation without increasing model size or inference-time sampling steps. This is more structured than ordinary augmentation because it regularizes the denoising dynamics themselves.

At a higher level, the model unifies world modeling, policy learning, and language planning at the parameter level rather than composing separate modules. The paper also stresses that the language and action experts are trained from scratch on top of a video-only backbone, without importing a pretrained language or reasoning model. That makes the comparison cleaner: gains are more attributable to the joint objective than to external language priors.74:T67c,The experiments span simulation and real-world manipulation. Three results stand out. First, on three compositional pick-and-place variants in MolmoSpaces, UniWALM improves average success by 14.8 points over the same-backbone FastWAM baseline. This is an important control because it keeps the visual backbone largely fixed and isolates the effect of joint language generation. Second, on the memory-dependent M(n) subset of RMBench, UniWALM reaches 34.5% versus 13.3% for same-backbone FastWAM, a gain of 21.2 points, and it also exceeds Mem-0 at 28.5%. The paper notes that UniWALM uses only a single anchor frame rather than privileged per-task keyframes, suggesting that textual memory plus a lightweight visual anchor already covers a meaningful part of long-horizon state tracking. Third, on a real-world bimanual Find-the-Item task, adding textual memory raises success from 11.1% to 61.1%, while compared VLA systems remain at or below 33.3%.

For ablations, the most important question is not just total score but which component contributes what: language generation, language feedback, anchor-frame memory, and FMC. The abstract already gives a strong signal that removing language hurts substantially even with the same backbone, and that textual memory matters most on memory-heavy tasks. When reading the full paper, it is worth checking whether the ablations separate: generating subtask text only, generating memory text only, generating language without feeding it back, and feeding it back without synchronous action generation. Those distinctions matter for deciding whether language is acting mainly as supervision or as functional memory.75:T46e,Start with three things. 1) The model is prompted to output a bounding box token span (<box> x1,y1,x2,y2 </box>) before producing rationale/answer—no external detector head.
2) After prefilling, visual patch tokens already reside in per-layer KV caches. Given the predicted box, LoRe maps it to the corresponding patch indices and amplifies their KV-cache entries, so subsequent autoregressive decoding attends more strongly to that region. This makes the newly identified evidence influence the current reasoning trajectory without generating extra visual tokens or waiting for a tool-returned crop.
3) RL training encourages selecting regions that support the final answer, effectively learning when/where to look while benefiting from the cache reweighting immediately.
Key distinction vs tool-based “thinking with images”: LoRe internalizes the visual operation as cache-level reweighting, avoiding multi-turn latency and token overhead, and removing the temporal mismatch where evidence only becomes available in the next turn.77:T674,The method has two layers. First, it evaluates rationale quality as certificate quality. A generated rationale is parsed into a directed acyclic graph of atomic claims and dependencies. Each claim is associated with a claim type, an evaluation criterion, polarity, and support relations. The certificate is then audited along three dimensions. Soundness checks whether claims are supported by the candidate responses and whether the rationale introduces false evidence or invalid comparisons. Coverage checks whether the rationale addresses the decision-relevant criteria specified by the evaluation policy rather than cherry-picking a few convenient points. Decision Support checks whether the local assessments made in the rationale are consistent with the final verdict, penalizing cases where the rationale argues for A but concludes B. Second, DeCert converts these audits into preference supervision. If two sampled judgments differ in verdict correctness, correctness dominates. If they share the same correct verdict, the model constructs rationale preference pairs based on certificate quality. This is the key design choice: it isolates rationale quality while holding outcome correctness fixed. Training then combines outcome-level and rationale-level preference optimization. Relative to RationaleRM, R-Align, and RM-NLHF, the main difference is that supervision is reference-free and based on validity of support rather than similarity to a target explanation. Another useful distinction is that DeCert exploits within-verdict variation among sampled judgments, which gives finer supervision than assigning a single scalar rationale score.78:T491,The empirical story has four main parts. First, on standard pairwise judgment benchmarks, DeCert consistently improves over strong generative judge baselines on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings, and the gains are not merely due to extra sampling because the paper compares under matched sampling budgets. Second, rationale-quality analyses show fewer unsupported claims, fewer omitted decision-relevant issues, and fewer verdict-rationale inconsistencies. Third, the positional-bias result is notable: without swap-based augmentation or explicit position-consistency supervision, DeCert improves position-consistent accuracy by up to 14.8 points over the corresponding base judges. This suggests that certificate auditing pushes the model toward content-grounded comparison rather than superficial A/B position cues. Fourth, ablations support the full design: all three certificate dimensions matter, verdict-only supervision is insufficient, and removing the same-verdict rationale preference construction weakens the gains substantially. The paper appears stronger on consistency of trends and analysis depth than on one dramatic headline number.79:T415,For a quick but useful read, focus on two questions: why reference rationales are the wrong supervision target, and why the paper treats a rationale as a certificate rather than just an explanation. About 25 to 35 minutes should be enough for a solid skim.7a:T66b,Ask-to-Distill (A2D) treats a prompt as a distribution elicitor: it determines which prefixes the student visits, hence where teacher token distributions become available for OPD.

Two-stage pipeline:
1) Train a prompt synthesizer before OPD.
- Initialize the synthesizer from the student.
- Optimize it with RL while keeping the scoring student and the teacher frozen.
- Crucially, the method avoids an expensive inner loop: it does not update the student per candidate prompt to estimate value.

2) A no-answer, distributional surrogate reward for prompt value.
- The reward aggregates token-level signals along student rollouts.
- Instead of rewarding pure disagreement (which can be dominated by support-mismatch), it uses a support-aware notion of teachability: combine teacher–student discrepancy with the teacher’s probability mass on the student’s candidate tokens, aiming to capture “corrective preference within student support” rather than “divergence outside support”.

Anti-gaming terms:
- Length control via sublinear length normalization plus a soft response-budget penalty to prevent inflating reward by longer outputs.
- A batch-level diversity term to prevent mode collapse into a narrow prompt family.

Curation:
- After training, prompts are format-filtered and lexically/semantically deduplicated; a frozen Qwen3-Embedding-4B is used only for semantic deduplication, not for reward computation.

Compared to synthetic SFT data, A2D does not need reference answers; compared to task-generation via success rewards, it optimizes the usability of teacher distributional supervision rather than task correctness.7b:T4a4,RACE has two core operations. Referential Abstraction removes identity-revealing text and replaces it with image-grounded references. These can be specific visual references, such as position, appearance, occlusion, or spatial relation, or ambiguous relational references that require searching over multiple depicted candidates and selecting the one whose retrieved evidence satisfies a condition. The construction searches all candidates, requires a unique match, rules out alternatives, and uses a question-only probe to detect identity or answer leakage. Compositional Evidence then builds questions whose answer depends on every selected target’s evidence. The targets can come from one image or from several images, and the construction requires that removing any designated contribution leaves the answer underdetermined. The data starts from real images, including social media photos, Bilibili video frames, and MovieNet imagery. For unannotated images, filtering, visual analysis, and retrieval establish candidate identities; MovieNet provides identity-image provenance. A teacher solves the resulting tasks, and only trajectories with correct final answers are kept for SFT.7c:T479,The authors build content-matched user requests and reply pairs. The dataset contains 287 first-person requests across six task types, rendered by local native speakers into several English varieties: Standard American English, British English, Australian English, African American English, Colloquial Singapore English, Nigerian Pidgin, Appalachian English, plus informal and formal Standard English controls. For outputs, they define a copy-controlled convergence ratio that scores only novel reply spans, excluding shared 4-grams and quoted text, so copying the user does not count as accommodation. For updates, they define a matching bonus using the length-normalized log-ratio between a stage and its preceding checkpoint. This measures whether the update assigns more gain to a matched reply for a user of variety v than for a Standard-English user. The paper also constructs calibrated accommodation pairs for DPO, penalizing under-accommodation, over-accommodation, and imposition.7d:T65a,DataPraxis is built around verified workspace evolution. The starting point is a seed workspace containing data assets and an execution environment. Instead of generating a task immediately from that initial directory, the framework lets an agent analyze the workspace, produce scripts, intermediate datasets, findings, and artifacts, and then writes verified results back into the workspace. This creates an evolved state that can support deeper follow-up analysis. Different analytical branches can also be inherited or combined, which allows later questions to depend on earlier discoveries.

Once a chain of findings and dependencies has been accumulated, the framework constructs a task backward from those dependencies. It removes the intermediate support that existed during workspace evolution, so the final solver must reconstruct the analysis from the raw materials. In this way, the hidden dependency structure discovered during evolution becomes a challenging long-horizon task.

To address reliability, the paper introduces dual-evidence verification. One source of evidence comes from validated findings produced during workspace evolution. The second comes from independent solution trajectories used to build and validate rubrics. The verifier therefore checks not only final answers but also deliverables, supporting evidence, and overall analytical quality. Compared with direct task generation from data descriptions, this approach is better at surfacing questions that only emerge after prior analysis. Compared with exploration-only task mining, it puts more emphasis on dependency accumulation and reuse.7e:T53c,The paper builds DataPraxis-5K, a dataset of 5,000 long-horizon professional analytics training examples across 15 domains, including business, finance, sports, and entertainment. A useful motivation experiment studies whether deeper questions really depend on prior analysis. When only the initial workspace is provided, mean perplexity rises from 16.87 to 31.07 for later rounds. When prior findings are also included, perplexity drops by 46.1% and 53.0% in rounds 2 and 3. This supports the paper’s main premise: deeper analytical questions are often not obvious from the raw workspace alone and become much more predictable once earlier findings are available.

From the provided full-content excerpt, however, the exact benchmarks, absolute scores, and strongest baselines are not yet visible, so those should be checked directly in the experimental section before drawing a stronger conclusion.7f:T6eb,The method, SpaRLax, has two main ingredients.

First, it builds stochastic but differentiable soft reasoning states. At each reasoning step, the model produces vocabulary logits, applies Gumbel reparameterization, and obtains a relaxed token distribution that can still support backpropagation. The key distinction from prior Gumbel-based soft-CoT methods is that the authors explicitly use the differentiability of the relaxation to restore gradient flow across reasoning steps. A soft token is therefore not treated as an opaque RL action; it becomes an internal node in the computation graph, allowing later losses and rewards to shape earlier soft reasoning choices through cross-step credit assignment.

Second, it introduces sparse relaxation. With a large LLM vocabulary, a dense softmax mixture spreads probability mass over many low-probability tokens, which injects long-tail noise into the mixed embedding and weakens reasoning focus. To address this, the paper replaces dense softmax with entmax on top of the Gumbel perturbation. Entmax can assign exact zeros to low-scoring tokens while preserving a continuous mixture over a small candidate set. This gives a better trade-off: it keeps the superposition capacity of soft reasoning but avoids the semantic blur of dense mixtures. The paper also argues that entmax adapts the degree of sparsity to uncertainty at each step, which is more principled than a hard top-k truncation.

Training is done in a controlled GRPO setup, using only final-answer rewards rather than supervised intermediate CoT labels. Evaluation is performed under both soft-CoT inference and standard hard-CoT inference. That choice is important: if gains transfer back to hard decoding, the method is more than a niche inference trick.80:T684,The experiments cover nine benchmarks spanning math, knowledge-intensive reasoning, and code reasoning. The main empirical result is that SpaRLax achieves the best weighted-average performance among compared soft-CoT post-training methods under a unified GRPO framework, and that this advantage appears under both soft and hard inference. That supports two claims: restoring cross-step gradients is better than treating soft tokens as non-differentiable actions, and the learned improvement is not confined to a special soft inference procedure.

The analysis sections appear to be more informative than the headline score. One set of analyses studies whether the model actually uses superposition in soft tokens, rather than collapsing to near one-hot pseudo-discrete states. This matters because many soft reasoning methods end up behaving like an expensive approximation to ordinary CoT. Another set studies sparsity. The paper reports that entmax consistently outperforms dense softmax across candidate-set settings, suggesting that suppressing long-tail vocabulary noise is not a minor implementation detail but a central requirement for making soft reasoning work in large-vocabulary LLMs.

The provided full-text excerpt does not include the complete numeric tables, model sizes, training budgets, or per-benchmark gains, so I cannot reliably state exact parameter counts or improvement margins. Those should be checked directly in the main results and appendix: base model scale, RL rollout configuration, reasoning length, Gumbel temperature, entmax alpha, and the exact hard-vs-soft decoding protocol all materially affect interpretation and reproducibility.81:T545,This is a skim-to-medium-depth paper. It is not necessary to follow every derivation, but a few parts deserve careful attention.

Start with the introduction and the problem framing. The important point is not the generic claim that soft CoT may be more expressive, but the authors' criticism that the usual RL formulation is mismatched: a soft token is not an element of the vocabulary action space, so treating it as a standard RL action is conceptually and algorithmically awkward. That observation drives the whole method.

Then read the method section closely enough to understand how gradients flow across reasoning steps. Two questions are worth keeping in mind: which parts of the objective use reparameterization gradients versus reward-based optimization, and whether the reasoning segment and final answer segment are optimized in the same way.

In the experiments, prioritize three things: the main results table, the superposition-versus-collapse analysis, and the entmax-versus-softmax ablation. If time is limited, focus on the fact that gains persist under hard inference, because that determines whether the method has value beyond a custom soft decoder. A useful first pass should take about 30–45 minutes. If you work on latent reasoning or RL for reasoning, the appendix is worth reading for training details and failure modes.82:T5ac,Gradus separates (a) deciding what behaviors to teach from (b) producing valid tasks/solutions that pass environment checks, via three components:
1) Guarded operators: for each action, represent its preconditions (state/policy guards), its possible policy-dependent outcomes, and how each outcome changes the state and future action requirements. This turns an environment’s latent rule structure into composable primitives.
2) Coverage-guided blueprint search: compose operators into structured task blueprints that specify which outcomes/interactions a task should exercise, with explicit controls over structural complexity. Maintain corpus-level coverage statistics and prioritize underrepresented outcomes and combinations, preventing global skew even if local task proposals look diverse.
3) Environment-grounded joint task–solution refinement: instead of discarding failed generations, use environment execution as a shared anchor to iteratively repair both the task (unsatisfiable constraints, hallucinated conditions, ambiguous goals) and the solution trajectory (policy violations, state-tracking errors). The blueprint constrains the repair so the intended behavioral coverage is preserved while making the instance verifiable.
The paper also varies “interaction dimensions” (ambiguity, indirect references, social pressure, extra reasoning burden) to decouple surface interaction difficulty from the underlying policy requirements.83:T510,Self-Credit is built on group-based RL, using a GRPO-like setup. For each query, the policy samples a group of trajectories, each receives a binary outcome reward, and a trajectory advantage is computed. Instead of applying this advantage uniformly to all tokens, Self-Credit introduces three components.

First, during rollouts, the policy generates summaries with citations to earlier turns that contain critical evidence. The summaries compact the long interaction history, while the citations become self-generated credit signals at the turn level.

Second, intra-group rescaling refines these credits. For the same prompt, the method compares cited turns across successful and failed rollouts. Turns that are repeatedly cited in successful trajectories and less common in failed ones receive stronger credit. Turns that also appear frequently in failed trajectories are downweighted or stripped of credit. This makes the signal less dependent on trusting the model’s citations in isolation.

Third, advantage reweighting applies the rescaled credit to the RL loss. Tokens inside highly credited turns receive stronger advantages, while unrelated turns receive less reinforcement. The method remains end-to-end and avoids training an additional critic or collecting dense human supervision.84:T4f8,The method is motivated by an empirical diagnostic: on student rollouts, correct answers show lower teacher–student KL on intermediate layer-to-layer transitions, with the strongest gaps for middle-to-late layer pairs, whereas final-layer agreement does not track correctness as well. OPTD augments OPD as follows:
- Keep the OPD objective: for each prefix visited by the student, compute token-level rewards from the teacher distribution (implemented over the student top-K candidates), corresponding to minimizing reverse KL from student to teacher on-policy.
- Add transition supervision: choose anchor layer pairs (a,b). For each candidate token v, compute a depthwise log-prob increment Δℓ(v; a→b)=log p_b(v|prefix) − log p_a(v|prefix). This captures both direction and magnitude of the teacher’s prediction revision across depth.
- Define a transition reward by comparing teacher vs student increments, and combine it with the standard final-layer OPD reward in a reward-weighted policy-gradient update.
Key distinction from prior work: it aligns predictive changes (logit/probability increments) rather than hidden representations, and turns layer-difference information (previously used mostly at decoding time) into a training-time distillation signal.85:T509,The method starts from the sampled-token log-ratio r_t = log pi_student(y_t | c_t) - log pi_teacher(y_t | c_t). In token-level OPD, positive r_t means the student assigns higher probability than the teacher to the sampled token, and the local advantage A_t = -stop_gradient(r_t) pushes that token down. The paper notes that positive log-ratios dominate the training signal: in the analyzed vanilla OPD rollouts, tokens with r_t > 0 account for 83.5% of the total absolute advantage mass. To reduce token-level noise, responses are divided into contiguous blocks. Each block is summarized by the mean positive log-ratio D_i. A penalty jump is an abrupt increase in D_i between adjacent blocks. The diagnostic analysis finds that such jumps persist on held-out tokens and coincide with lower teacher confidence, measured by higher entropy and lower top-1 probability. AP-OPD responds by scaling down all signed supervision coefficients in the block after a detected jump. The preceding block serves as a local reference, and the scale is chosen so that the weighted average penalty of the post-jump block matches the previous block’s original mean. The rule preserves signs and relative token weights, introduces no extra strength hyperparameter, and requires no additional forward passes.86:T5e2,The method starts from the SVD of a frozen pretrained weight matrix W0 = UΣV^T. Let Uk and Vk be the top-k left and right singular vectors. OPLoRA constructs two orthogonal projectors onto the complementary subspaces: PL = I - UkUk^T and PR = I - VkVk^T. Standard LoRA uses a low-rank update ΔW = (α/r)BA. OPLoRA replaces it with a doubly projected update, ΔW = PL·B·A·PR. This forces the learned update to live entirely outside the dominant singular subspaces of the pretrained weight.

The main technical claim is stronger than a regularization heuristic: under this construction, the top-k singular triples of the original weight are exactly preserved. In other words, the update cannot perturb that protected spectral structure. This is a meaningful distinction from methods that only penalize parameter drift, approximate importance with Fisher-style terms, or rely on replay. OPLoRA constrains the reachable update space itself.

The paper also introduces a subspace-interference metric, ρk, to quantify how much update energy lies in the dominant pretrained subspace. Even from the provided excerpt, it is clear that the metric is meant to connect geometry and forgetting: ordinary LoRA should exhibit nontrivial alignment with the top-k subspace, while OPLoRA should suppress it by construction. The practical trade-off is straightforward. The method requires SVD on target layers and a choice of k. If k is too large, adaptation capacity shrinks; if k is too small, protection may be weak.87:T44b,This is a good skim paper: the core idea is simple, and the main question is whether the theory and experiments line up. Start with the setup and the central assumption that important pretrained knowledge is concentrated in dominant singular directions. Then read the definition of OPLoRA carefully and make sure the need for double-sided projection is clear; a one-sided projection would not protect both row and column subspaces in the same way.

After that, go to the theorem that claims exact preservation of the top-k singular triples. That result is the backbone of the paper. In the experiments, prioritize the retention-versus-adaptation tables, the ρk analysis, and the ablations over k, rank, and insertion locations. Also check how “knowledge retention” is operationalized, because the strength of the conclusion depends on whether retention is measured by general benchmarks, held-out capabilities, or some narrower proxy. A 20-30 minute read should be enough to capture the main idea; spend more time only if you care about continual fine-tuning, PEFT theory, or adapter stability.88:T9a6,方法设计很克制，核心是把“能力存在”与“组合后退化”严格分开。作者先从同一数据集抽取独立任务，要求模型在单题条件下已经答对，再把这些任务按固定模板直接串接成一个 prompt，形成大小为 k 的 composition。这样做避免了任务改写、提示变化、跨任务依赖等混杂因素，确保唯一变化是同一响应里要同时处理的任务数。随后按 task 级别计算 accuracy drop：比较某题在 k-way composition 中的正确率与 isolation 中的正确率差值，并用多次采样估计。

机制分析分两步。第一步是排除独立错误累积。若每题在 isolation 中失败概率为 p_i，那么组合后的退化若只是累积效应，per-task 正确率不应显著低于其单题水平；但作者观察到的 drop 明显更大，说明组合改变了每个子任务本身的求解过程。第二步是定位预算机制。作者统计模型在不同 composition size 下为每个任务实际生成的 reasoning token，发现随着 k 增大，平均每题 token 数系统性下降，并且近似 obey power-law scaling。这里的关键不是总输出长度触顶，而是在远未达到 context/output 上限时，模型仍然主动把每题“想”的篇幅压短。

在 fragile task 的定义上，作者不是凭任务类型先验划分，而是用经验退化模式来识别：某些题在不同随机采样、不同 composition size 下反复表现出更大 drop，这些题构成模型特定的 fragile 子集。全文进一步表明，这些 fragile 题在 isolation 中往往就有更长的 reasoning trace，说明它们更依赖充足的 test-time compute。值得注意的是，fragility 在同一模型内部相对稳定，但跨模型不完全一致，意味着这不是数据集固有难度，而是模型内部表征与推理策略共同决定的属性。

基于这个发现，作者提出 fragility-aware batching。它不改模型、不需要 logits 或内部状态，是纯黑盒策略：先通过经验测量估计任务 fragility，再按 fragility 把题分到不同 batch size。非 fragile 题放大 batch，让隐式预算自动压缩每题 token；fragile 题放小 batch，保留足够思考空间。它和常规“全都单独做”相比更省 token，和“全都大 batch”相比更稳。这个方法的意义不在算法复杂度，而在于它把一个认知层面的缺陷转成了可操作的 inference policy。89:T977,The experimental design is the main strength. The authors separate capability existence from composition-induced degradation. They first select tasks that the model already solves correctly in isolation. They then leave those tasks unchanged and simply concatenate them into a single prompt using a fixed dataset-specific template. This removes confounds such as paraphrasing, task reformulation, or inter-task dependencies. The only manipulated variable is how many tasks share one response.

They measure task-level accuracy drop by comparing each task’s accuracy at composition size k against its isolated accuracy, using multiple trials for estimation. This lets them ask whether composition changes the model’s ability on the constituent task itself, not just the aggregate prompt success rate.

The mechanism analysis proceeds in two stages. First, they rule out independent error accumulation as a sufficient explanation. If each task merely retained its isolated failure probability, the observed per-task degradation should be much smaller than what they actually measure. Second, they analyze reasoning-token allocation. As k increases, the model systematically emits fewer reasoning tokens per task, and this reduction follows an approximate power law. The important point is that this happens even when the total response remains comfortably below the model’s explicit output limit, so the effect is not simple truncation.

They then define fragile tasks empirically rather than by task category. Some tasks repeatedly suffer larger drops across sampling noise and across composition sizes. These tasks also tend to have longer reasoning traces in isolation, which supports the interpretation that they are more sensitive to reduced test-time compute. Fragility is relatively stable within a model but differs across models, suggesting that it is not just dataset difficulty; it depends on the model’s internal representations and reasoning policy.

Based on this, the paper proposes fragility-aware batching. It is a black-box inference strategy: estimate task fragility empirically, batch non-fragile tasks more aggressively to exploit the model’s tendency to shorten reasoning, and keep fragile tasks in smaller batches so they retain enough budget. The contribution is modest algorithmically but strong conceptually: a weakness in budget allocation is converted into a practical scheduling policy.8a:T72f,The study spans eight datasets across mathematical and linguistic settings. Two are constructed by the authors: 1,000 indefinite integrals with symbolic verification, and OneWordQA, a factual QA set with single-word or numeric answers and minimal reasoning demand. The rest include established benchmarks such as GPQA-Diamond, GSM8K, and MATH-500. The model suite includes strong open-weight models as well as Claude Opus 5.

The first main result is that composition-induced degradation is robust. Even when only tasks solved correctly in isolation are used, per-task accuracy drops substantially as more tasks are concatenated, and the drop is much larger than what independent error accumulation would predict. This holds across both math-heavy and language-heavy datasets.

The second result is the token-allocation pattern. Reasoning tokens per task decrease systematically with composition size and approximately follow a power-law trend. Since the full response is still far from the model’s hard sequence limit, this is evidence for an internal budget-allocation behavior rather than explicit truncation.

The third result is the characterization of fragility. Tasks with longer isolated reasoning traces are more likely to be fragile under composition. Fragility is stable within a model across random trials and composition sizes, but the fragile subset is not the same across models.

The most actionable result is fragility-aware batching. Relative to solving every task separately, it reduces generated tokens by about 43% on average across datasets with no accuracy loss. The same idea transfers to a proprietary frontier model: on GPQA-Diamond with Claude Opus 5, generated tokens drop by 24% without degrading performance. That makes the paper relevant not only for evaluation but also for practical inference scheduling.8b:T574,Start with the problem setup in the introduction and the early part of Section 3. The crucial point is that the paper is not measuring multi-task prompt success in the usual loose sense; it is measuring whether tasks already known to be solvable remain solvable after concatenation. That controlled setup is the foundation of the whole argument.

Then read the analysis of reasoning tokens in Section 3.1 carefully, especially the figures showing per-task token allocation versus composition size. First, the authors adapt causal tracing to masked DLMs. The clean input masks the object span, matching the model’s training objective. The corrupted input masks both subject and object, removing the factual cue. Internal states are restored from the clean run into the corrupted run, and the indirect effect measures how much the correct masked-object prediction recovers. In the experiments, a base model is trained on ground-truth demonstrations, then wrapped with a scaffold to form a teacher. A same-class, same-size student is trained on the teacher’s traces, either from scratch or by fine-tuning the base model. The tasks include Dyck languages, Sokoban, and modular arithmetic. The scaffolds include verifier-guided backtracking, A* search with model-pruned expansions, and a simpler fixed-token-deletion regeneration rule. The key experimental design separates local competence from compositional competence: the base model can perform the local steps, while the scaffold maintains candidates, search frontiers, visited sets, or verifier-controlled backtracking state. The theoretical part models search through directed s-t reachability. The base model answers local edge queries, which are computable by constant-depth Boolean circuits. The scaffold repeatedly uses these local queries to run BFS and decide reachability. Internalizing the scaffold requires the student to decide reachability from the graph representation. Under standard precision assumptions, fixed-depth polynomial-size Transformers can be simulated by TC0 circuits, even with logarithmic-length chain-of-thought in the cited setting. Directed reachability gives the separation: the external harness computes a closure over local primitives that the restricted student model need not represent.8f:T479,Across the controlled tasks, same-size students do not close the gap to the scaffolded teacher, especially out of distribution. Training from scratch and fine-tuning the base model both leave a substantial gap. Increasing the student size changes the picture: sufficiently large students match and eventually surpass the fixed teacher, supporting the capacity-based explanation. Replacing verifier-controlled backtracking with a simpler fixed deletion-and-regeneration scaffold makes the behavior much easier to internalize; the same-size student can match that simpler teacher. The first is Iterative Orthogonal Subspace Decomposition. Instead of learning one linear probe, the method learns multiple orthogonal directions sequentially. After extracting one direction, it removes the already explained deceptive signal and searches for the next direction in the residual space. The goal is to capture complementary components of deception rather than redundant variants of the same feature. The second component is a Domain-Adaptive Gating Mechanism. Static combinations of these directions are not sufficient because a direction that is informative in one domain may be irrelevant or noisy in another. DDSN therefore uses a small amount of test-time few-shot adaptation to assign context-dependent weights to the extracted directions. In effect, the detector asks which deception components are active in the current domain, rather than whether one universal deception vector is present. Relative to standard single-direction probing, the key difference is not just moving from one dimension to k dimensions, but making the composition itself adaptive to context.91:T499,The main empirical claim is straightforward: single-direction probes can work within a dataset but generalize poorly across heterogeneous deception settings, supporting the paper’s argument that deception feature composition depends on context. DDSN achieves stronger and more stable performance across datasets. The headline numbers in the abstract are an average AUROC of 0.97 and 95% recall at 5% FPR with only 10 adaptation examples. The paper also claims that transfer across related domains can work without re-adaptation, and that the 10-example adaptation is only needed when there is a substantial context shift, which can be flagged by a lightweight classifier. The most important evidence, if supported in the full text, would be ablations on the number of subspace directions, comparisons across layers, tests against simpler multi-probe baselines such as PCA-style decompositions or static ensembles, and adaptation curves showing how much the gating mechanism buys over fixed combinations. The paper’s credibility depends less on the absolute numbers and more on whether the datasets are diverse enough to genuinely invalidate the single-direction assumption.92:Ta82,The setup is intentionally simple enough for mechanistic analysis. The task is to take K distinct integers, followed by a SEP token, and autoregressively output them in sorted order. Most experiments train at K=16 and evaluate across lengths from 2 up to N. The model is a two-layer, single-head, causally masked transformer with no positional encodings. Removing positional encodings is not just a simplification choice; it avoids a structural barrier to length generalization and prevents the model from relying on absolute-position-specific strategies.

The central finding is that training converges to two solution classes. One is effectively single-stage: the second attention layer can be ablated with little or no effect, so most of the sorting logic is implemented without meaningful second-layer participation. The other is genuinely two-stage: both layers matter, and ablating the second layer hurts performance. This second class generalizes almost perfectly to longer sequences.

The mechanistic analysis of the two-stage solution has two main components. First is cross-layer specialization. The two layers are not redundant; they appear to divide labor, especially on cases where adjacent sorted numbers have small gaps. The paper defines the gap as the difference between consecutive sorted elements and argues that small-gap cases are relatively rare at K=16 but become increasingly common as sequence length grows. A model that does not learn to handle these cases robustly can look perfect in-distribution and still fail under length extrapolation. Second is a hinting mechanism. The first layer appears to narrow the set of plausible next tokens or provide a structured intermediate signal, and the second layer then selects among these candidates. As the number of possible candidates grows with input length, this staged procedure is more stable than a flatter one-layer-style selection rule.

The paper also studies why one algorithm emerges instead of the other. A key result is that layer-wise initialization scale can strongly bias training toward the single-stage or two-stage solution. That matters because it shows the bifurcation is not merely a post hoc interpretability story; it is tied to controllable early training dynamics. The authors also test minimum-finding and a greedy coin denomination task. Minimum-finding shows the opposite pattern, where the simpler solution generalizes better, while the coin task exhibits a broader mix of behaviors. So the lesson is not that deeper or more complex solutions always generalize better, but that generalization depends on task structure, rare-pattern statistics, and whether layers learn complementary roles.93:T647,The experimental setup is compact but sufficient. The main configuration trains at K=16 with online sampling, batch size 4096, AdamW, learning rate 0.03, for 60,000 iterations. Models reach 100% training accuracy early and are then trained further to near-zero loss. Evaluation sweeps sequence length from 2 to N, with the main focus on extrapolation beyond the training length.

Three results matter most. First, different seeds reliably land in two mechanistically distinct solution classes under the same objective, and these classes are cleanly separated by second-layer attention ablation: one class barely uses the second layer, the other depends on it. Second, the gap in length generalization is large. The two-stage solutions remain nearly perfect beyond the training length, while the effectively single-stage solutions degrade substantially despite fitting the training length equally well. Third, the failure mode is tied to gap statistics: small-gap inputs become more frequent at longer lengths, and the two-stage solutions are more robust on exactly those cases. The excerpt provided does not include all tables and exact numbers, but the qualitative claim is strong: this is not a marginal improvement but a split between near-perfect extrapolation and systematic failure.

The most informative ablations are layer ablation, initialization-scale steering, and task transfer to minimum-finding and greedy coin denomination. The authors test whether the problem is crowding in busy directions and find instead that the digit-induced change is small. Random noise lands in similarly busy directions, while replacing the digit with a random word moves the state much more and is readable. For computed values, the paper proposes a stricter protocol: compare a candidate value against what input-copy traces allow, rank candidates under a prime modulus, check sign-flipped twins, and compare against answer mixtures and synthetic generic mixing. The setup uses a neutral prompt such as "{} is known for" and computes a linear readout at a fixed layer for entities of type t. Unlike an LRE, the entity lens does not use a relation template, does not use object supervision, and does not rely on subject-object pairs.

The paper studies two variants. The contrastive entity lens (CEL) uses differences between the target entity state and reference entity states, aiming to capture what is distinctive about the entity relative to others of the same type. The non-contrastive entity lens (NEL) drops that differencing because CEL turns out to be sensitive to the choice of reference set. For example, reference entities with different nationalities can artificially amplify or suppress nationality-related tokens.

The prediction target is not the gold object but LRE faithfulness: the rate at which the affine LRE decoder reproduces the model’s own top-1 prediction. The authors then ask whether entity-lens scores, computed without any relation information, can predict faithfulness across relations. They also run leave-one-type-out tests and controls for object cardinality and answer-token frequency to check whether the effect is merely driven by shallow dataset properties.

A useful additional contribution is methodological. The paper shifts part of the analysis from the relation level to the individual-fact level and argues that existing datasets contain artifacts that obscure progress, especially semantically weak first tokens and reference competition among plausible outputs.97:T5aa,The proposed method is NR-SAE, a native-router sparse autoencoder. Each routed expert owns a small dictionary. When the frozen MoE router selects an expert for a token, the corresponding dictionary is opened; dictionaries for unselected experts are not scored. This differs from global SAEs over the summed MoE output and from approaches that learn a separate auxiliary router for the SAE.

The paper tests the factorization at two seams. In the reconstructive seam, the SAE receives a selected expert’s raw output yt,s and reconstructs it. In the predictive seam, a transcoder receives the common MoE input xt and predicts the selected expert’s output. The first setting tests whether expert outputs admit expert-local dictionaries; the second tests whether these dictionaries can capture the expert’s computation from its input.

The controls are carefully designed. Layout A is the native router-addressed design: 128 experts, each with a 512-feature bank; with eight routed experts per token, a token sees 4,096 candidates and selects 32 slots. Layout F matches A in total stored features and parameters but uses rank banks with many more candidates per bank. Layout B matches A in visible candidate count but groups by routing rank rather than expert identity. Layout R keeps A’s architecture but applies a per-sequence bijection from expert IDs to bank IDs, preserving grouping and capacity while destroying stable expert-bank identity.98:T49f,The main checkpoint is Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, with 28 layers, hidden size 1536, vocabulary size 151,936, and 32,768 model position embeddings.
