Trajectory-informed interventions also produce more target-specific changes in internal dominance endpoints than fixed or matched shuffled policies.99:T791,The core idea is to identify cross-modal concept neurons. The authors adopt the key-value memory view of Transformer FFNs and treat individual FFN neurons as fine-grained units that can encode concept-selective directions. For a given label, such as angry, they run one forward pass with an audio example plus a question prompt, and another with a text description corresponding to the expected answer, such as “The speaker feels angry.” They then identify neurons that are strongly associated with that label on the audio side and on the text side, and measure their overlap.

If a shared subspace exists, matching audio-text label pairs should overlap in these label-relevant neurons more than mismatching pairs. This is the central departure from prior work that compares full hidden vectors using cosine similarity. The authors show that ambient-space similarity is dominated by dimensions unrelated to the label and therefore has weak discriminative value for concept alignment.

To move beyond correlation, they perform two causal interventions. First, they use steering: they shift activations along directions derived from text-side cross-modal neurons and test whether audio-based recognition moves toward the target label. Second, they deactivate the identified neurons by zeroing them out and check whether the target task degrades before unrelated tasks do. This makes the claim much stronger: text-defined internal directions can causally alter audio recognition, and the shared neurons are functionally necessary for at least part of the model’s cross-modal behavior.

Compared with earlier interpretability work, the paper is more specific in three ways. It does not just track where audio information flows across layers. It does not only identify audio-specific neurons. And it does not rely on probing alone. It asks whether audio and text meet in the same internal units, and tests that claim with interventions.9a:T73e,The study covers three LALMs: Qwen2.5-Omni, DeSTA2.5-Audio, and Audio Flamingo 3, across four attribute types: animal sound, emotion, gender, and spoken language. Several quantitative findings stand out.

First, cosine similarity between full hidden vectors is a poor signal for label matching. The authors report that label-independent dimensions account for 88% to 100% of its variance, which explains why matching and mismatching audio-text label pairs are barely separable in ambient space. This is an important negative result because it directly challenges a common way of arguing for multimodal alignment.

Second, in steering experiments, text-derived cross-modal neuron directions alter audio recognition much more effectively than random neuron sets. For Qwen2.5-Omni and Audio Flamingo 3, this holds for 35 of 48 labels; for DeSTA2.5-Audio, for 7 of 24 labels. A striking example is that Qwen2.5-Omni can be pushed to answer “happy” for silent inputs: the unsteered baseline is 20%, while the best random neuron set reaches 45%, and the targeted steering is substantially stronger.

Third, deactivating the cross-modal neurons damages the target attribute task before unrelated tasks. This pattern holds in all 8 task combinations for Qwen2.5-Omni and Audio Flamingo 3, and in 2 of 4 for DeSTA2.5-Audio. In Qwen2.5-Omni, deactivating only 0.2% to 0.7% of FFN neurons is enough to cause damage comparable to removing the most audio-specific neurons, even though the cross-modal neurons are less audio-specific. That suggests they occupy a bottleneck position for integrating acoustic attributes into the text-anchored semantic machinery.

The weaker effects in DeSTA2.5-Audio are plausibly explained by its use of ASR transcripts, which may let the model partially bypass the pure audio pathway and dilute the causal role of shared neurons.9b:T4eb,Start with the introduction and pay attention to the critique of cosine similarity. First, an ordinal granularity router predicts the appropriate disclosure level. The target is modeled as an ordered label space, such as A/B/C, ranging from abstention or very coarse disclosure to country/city level and then precise location disclosure. The router operates on a pre-generation hidden representation, typically the hidden state of the final prompt token at a chosen decoder layer. Using linear probing and ordinal regression, the paper shows that disclosure levels are recoverable and arranged along a common direction in representation space. This motivates projecting the hidden state onto a disclosure-granularity coordinate and routing it to a target level.

Second, a steering module applies route-specific hidden-state interventions during decoding so that the generated answer better matches the routed granularity. The framework is inference-time only: it does not require a separately fine-tuned model for each policy and does not depend on demonstration-heavy prompting. Compared with prompting, it acts more directly on internal generation dynamics; compared with training-based methods, it is cheaper to deploy and easier to adapt.

Technically, this is best understood as a representation-analysis-plus-activation-steering paper. The main novelty is treating contextual privacy as an ordered routing problem rather than a flat safe/unsafe classification task.9d:T444,The experiments cover multiple VLM backbones. The first important result is the probing analysis: linear probes trained on pre-generation hidden states outperform the model’s raw responses on contextual disclosure alignment metrics. That shows the appropriate disclosure level is often encoded internally even when the model does not express it reliably.

The paper then demonstrates that disclosure levels exhibit an ordered structure along a shared representation direction, which supports the router design. In the main evaluation, the route-and-steer framework improves contextual disclosure alignment over unmodified models and baselines, while better balancing over-disclosure and under-disclosure and incurring only modest alignment tax. The method also generalizes to DoxBench, suggesting the intervention is not tied to a single benchmark distribution.

For a foundation-model reader, the most informative result is not the absolute benchmark score but the gap between probe performance and response behavior, and the fact that inference-time steering can partially close that gap.9e:T415,This is a skim paper. Start with the motivating study and the representation analysis. The two claims to verify are: first, whether pre-generation hidden states really contain the target disclosure signal; second, whether that signal has a stable ordinal geometry. If those claims are weak, the rest reduces to a task-specific steering trick.

Then read the method section on the router and the steering intervention. The useful questions are why the authors use ordinal routing instead of standard classification, and why they choose inference-time intervention instead of training a new policy head. In the experiments, focus on probe-versus-response comparisons, the main alignment table, and the breakdown between over- and under-disclosure. Expected reading time is 20 to 30 minutes.

From a pretraining-oriented perspective, the main lesson is that internal representations and final behavior can be systematically mismatched. A recoverable signal in hidden states does not guarantee that the model will naturally use it during generation.9f:T87e,The method has three main components. First is the definition and measurement of k*. Each task is cast as binary or one-vs-rest classification over frozen LM representations. A dense linear probe provides a reference AUROC C. The authors then search over subsets of representation coordinates and define k* as the smallest feature count whose best sparse probe recovers 95% of the dense probe’s performance above chance. The point is not to solve the optimal sparse selection problem exactly, but to use a fixed, reproducible protocol that supports comparisons across tasks and models. Second is cross-model feature correspondence. Similar k* values alone do not imply that models rely on similar features. To probe that, the paper uses sparse autoencoder features and compares the responses of selected task-relevant SAE features across models on shared inputs. The analysis controls for two easy confounds: label correlation and class-mean differences. On several tasks, selected features show stronger cross-model response correspondence than matched controls, suggesting some input-level alignment in the readout structure. Third is training intervention and downstream prediction. The paper compares base models with their instruction-tuned counterparts, and separately varies weights and input format to disentangle where changes in readout sparsity come from. Both matter, and the interaction is task-dependent. To isolate the role of target supervision, the authors run controlled synthetic experiments with binary factors. They create target aggregates paired with correct labels and control aggregates paired with random labels. Learned targets often admit single-feature readouts, while readable controls still require tens of features, even when controls share half their factors with a trained target. This supports the claim that supervision can compress a target into a direct linear direction without equivalently compressing related structure. Finally, k* is tested as a diagnostic for label requirements in student adaptation, for distinguishing head failure from representational loss after continual learning, and for understanding pruning sensitivity.a0:T85c,The study evaluates 19 language models from five labs on 14 core tasks. Several results stand out. First, across 10 base models, the nine tasks with consistently strong dense-probe performance have very similar k* rankings, with a median cross-lab Spearman correlation of 0.93. Some intent classification tasks need only 4–5 residual coordinates to recover most of the dense-probe signal, indicating highly concentrated task readouts. Second, on three tasks, selected SAE features show cross-model response correspondence beyond what is explained by matched label correlation, and this remains after removing class-mean differences. That is stronger evidence than simple probe agreement because it operates at the level of responses to individual inputs. Third, instruction tuning selectively reduces k*, but not uniformly across tasks. Additional experiments show that both weight changes and prompt/input format contribute to this effect. Fourth, in the synthetic supervision setup, successfully learned targets often become readable from a single feature, whereas control variables remain diffuse and require tens of features even when they overlap substantially with the target factors. Fifth, across eight student models, reference-model k* predicts the number of labels needed for supervised adaptation, following an empirical relation N* ∝ (k*)^0.65. This is one of the most practically relevant findings because it links representational sparsity to sample efficiency. Sixth, after continual learning, old classification heads can fail while dense probes remain near baseline, implying that some apparent forgetting is head mismatch rather than complete loss of linear readability. Recovery also needs fewer labels than initial learning under the tested setup. Seventh, under pruning, dense-probe performance drops, and wider pre-pruning readouts tend to suffer larger losses. However, interventions based on allocating labels by feature count or protecting parameters associated with selected readout features do not consistently beat the baselines, so k* looks more mature as a diagnostic than as a direct intervention target.a1:T4b8,If reading selectively, start with the introduction, the figure defining k*, the main base-model comparison, the instruction-tuning analysis, the synthetic supervision experiment, and the continual-learning/pruning results. The most important section to read carefully is the measurement protocol. The interpretation of k* depends heavily on the feature search, confirmation, and aggregation procedure, and on the choice to recover 95% of dense-probe-above-chance performance. The second key section is the cross-model SAE analysis: check how correspondence is defined and how class-mean artifacts are removed. The third is the training and downstream section, where the paper moves from description to mechanism and prediction. Two useful questions to keep in mind are: whether k* is mostly a property of the task geometry or a product of training trajectory, and whether it could become an early diagnostic during pretraining rather than only a post hoc analysis tool. Good follow-up angles include layerwise behavior of k*, sensitivity to tokenizer or architecture choice, and whether SAE correspondence really indicates shared semantic basis functions rather than merely shared discriminative directions.a2:T58f,REM (Reusable Experience Memory) introduces three explicit decisions, executed from within the agent’s loop:
1) What to store:
- Each completed run is a 55K–170K token trajectory with heavy exploration noise.
- REM consolidates it into a phase-structured document organized by four phases: localize, understand, fix, verify. This document is both the retrieval unit and the primary injected context, avoiding duplicated token spending.
- The design choice is deliberate: not raw trajectories (too noisy and context-hungry), not atomized factoids (lose solution structure).
2) When to recall:
- Two-tier read path: the phase document is injected at task start; a much costlier “implementation record” (fine-grained details closer to the original trace) is withheld.
- A struggle-gated in-loop node injects the implementation record only when the running agent appears stuck, leveraging the fact that the agent state is observable only inside the loop.
3) What to forget:
- The implementation record is evicted after a single exposure (one-shot eviction) to prevent persistent bias; the phase document remains for the whole run.
Additionally, the only domain-specific artifact is an extraction schema, which the paper claims can be automatically discovered from example trajectories. Ablations are framed to show gains come mainly from the stored form, while gating/eviction prevent the second tier from causing harm.a3:T406,AscendEvolve couples platform knowledge with evolutionary kernel search. The system has three main design choices. First, it builds a hierarchical and version-aware corpus from documentation, headers, and vendor operator libraries, then distills it into per-operator evidence before search. This avoids repeatedly processing a large heterogeneous corpus. Second, it uses demand-driven retrieval: concrete implementation or optimization questions are routed to a small set of relevant sources instead of placing broad documentation into the prompt. Third, it creates bidirectional interaction between retrieved knowledge and execution experience. Retrieved mechanisms seed candidate implementations; compilation, execution, and profiling provide empirical verdicts on the evidence used; these verdicts influence later retrieval and search. The evolutionary search maintains multiple mechanism-distinct implementation lines, so the agent can explore different implementation families rather than prematurely committing to one route.a4:T41e,The buyers are Claude Code and Codex. Sellers are run with five production model-agent stacks: Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, DeepSeek Harness, and Antigravity. Under all seller models, descriptions are repeatedly rewritten and come to claim more fields than the original vendor descriptions. The added claims include fields returned by the tool for fewer than half of the targets. Four seller models show mild toolflation, mostly adding fields seen in their own example output, though they do not remove contradicted claims. One model shows severe toolflation, including fields absent from its own output and copying language from highly selected competitors. Market allocation changes materially: in seven of ten seller-model/platform combinations, the strongest tool ends at least ten percentage points below its share under vendor descriptions. Under severe toolflation, weak tools receive substantial traffic. On Amazon, buyer task success drops from 89% to about 30%, close to the 28% random-choice baseline; on Instagram it drops from 77% to 40%.a5:T766,The contribution is a controlled transfer test rather than a new agent architecture. The authors use τ²-bench, a standard dual-control benchmark spanning airline, retail, and telecom domains. In airline and retail, tools are available only to the agent; in telecom, the user also has tools and can act on the shared environment. The comparison is between the benchmark’s stock single-agent system and a centralized multi-agent system built from the same base model. The MAS has three roles: an orchestrator that plans and talks to the user, a database agent that executes reads and writes, and a policy advisor that helps with compliance. This choice is deliberate: it keeps the MAS architecture relatively deployable instead of relying on unconstrained research-style multi-agent chatter.

Several design choices are methodologically important. First, the primary analysis uses a capability index measured on held-out domains, rather than regressing MAS gain directly on the same-cell SAS score. This avoids the mechanical negative slope that can appear when gain is regressed on its own baseline. Second, the MAS is evaluated under a per-episode completion-token ceiling calibrated from the SAS’s own spend, and the paper also reports what happens when that ceiling is removed. Third, the study includes mechanical validity checks to separate “MAS does not help” from “the MAS is broken.” Fourth, the work is pre-registered, with code, prompts, configurations, change logs, and trajectories released. That makes the result more credible as a systems experiment.

So the technical value lies in evaluation design and causal hygiene, not in proposing a better MAS. The paper reframes the question from “do more agents make the system smarter?” to “under user interaction, budget constraints, and realistic interface structure, does coordination still produce net benefit?”a6:T772,The study covers 6 models from 3 families across 3 domains, giving 18 model-by-domain cells, of which 16 were run on the registered configuration, for roughly 7,950 simulated conversations in total. Within each cell, SAS and MAS are run on the same 50 tasks with 3 random seeds. The main findings are straightforward.

First, under a fixed simulated user, no cell shows a MAS benefit. Among the 13 cells that pass the mechanical validity bars, MAS is worse than SAS in 12 and tied in the remaining one. The weighted mean gain is about -28 points. That is a large enough effect to suggest that coordination overhead and interaction friction dominate any benefit from specialization in this setting.

Second, the earlier capability-saturation rule would predict MAS gains in two low-capability cells, but the observed results are losses of 13 and 22 points. So even the “MAS should help when SAS is weak” part does not transfer here.

Third, removing the budget ceiling does not rescue the MAS in a meaningful way. At best it reaches parity, and only at about 5.5 times the SAS median token spend. This indicates that the issue is not merely an overly tight budget; the architecture struggles to convert extra compute into reliable task gains.

Fourth, the paper does not find evidence that MAS gain declines with capability in this design, but it also does not overclaim the opposite. The slope test detects no dependence, yet the interval remains wide because model-family and domain effects dominate the between-cell variation. That is a careful and appropriate interpretation.

Fifth, simulator choice matters a lot. In the cell nearest the previously suggested 45% crossover, the result is only a tie under one simulator, but switching the simulator can produce a 10-point gain. This means user simulation is itself a major source of variance and can materially change the MAS-versus-SAS conclusion.a7:T4f2,This is a skim paper. Focus on the experimental design, not the literature review. Start with the introduction and pin down the exact claim under test: the transferability of the capability-saturation principle from autonomous benchmarks to dual-control settings. Then go straight to the setup section and inspect three things carefully: what the centralized MAS actually looks like, how the token budget is calibrated, and how the capability index is defined. Those choices determine whether the comparison is fair.

Next, read the main result tables and the slope analysis. You want to verify three points: the absolute MAS-minus-SAS differences, which cells pass the mechanical validity checks, and whether relaxing the budget changes the qualitative outcome. If all three line up, the negative result is robust.

Finally, read the simulator-sensitivity discussion. The durable takeaway is not “MAS never helps,” but that dual-control evaluation is much more fragile than autonomous evaluation, and conclusions depend on user models, interaction protocol, and deployability constraints. A useful skim should take about 25 to 35 minutes. If you work on agent benchmarks or tool-use systems, the preregistration and statistical appendix are worth an extra pass.a8:T428,ClawMMU attaches a protection descriptor to every memory representation. The descriptor records owner, scope, origins, and authority. Authority is ordered: tool outputs and fetched documents can be marked as Evidence, meaning readable but not actionable, while user-approved instructions can have Policy-level authority. Derived memory follows an inheritance rule: it receives no more authority than the least trusted input, its usable scope is restricted to where all inputs are valid, and its origins include all source pages. The model itself is treated as a low-authority input because generated summaries can be steered by injected text. Authority can only be raised by the owner through explicit approval or pre-authorized approval. The system checks descriptors at four boundaries: map when new external content enters context, derive when content is written to storage, reload when stored content returns, and authorize when content drives a tool call or external action. Revocation counters invalidate derived memories when a source page is later revoked.a9:T6c6,The setup models an agent as a fixed solver model M paired with a harness H, where H controls prompting, context management, tool interaction, and execution logic. The central analytical tool is pass@k. pass@1 is treated as a proxy for single-run reliability, while pass@k measures the fraction of tasks solved at least once within k attempts and is used as a proxy for coverage. The key logic is simple: if an optimized harness only improves reliability on already-solvable tasks, its advantage should shrink or even reverse as k increases. If it truly expands the solvable set, the advantage should persist at larger k.

For optimization, the paper uses Meta-Harness. A coding agent proposes harness revisions after inspecting prior harness code, evaluation scores, and execution traces. Candidate harnesses are validated, and the best one H* is compared against the initial harness H0. The novelty is less in the optimizer itself than in the evaluation lens applied to the resulting harnesses.

The paper also introduces stronger references: larger models from the same family and settings with higher reasoning effort. This makes the comparison more informative. It asks whether harness optimization merely makes a smaller model look better at low attempt budgets, or whether it actually approaches the task coverage of stronger systems. Results are further broken down by task difficulty and OOD conditions, which is important because aggregate scores can hide losses on harder subsets.

Methodologically, the strongest part of the paper is this multi-axis diagnosis: attempt budget, task difficulty, OOD behavior, and comparison to stronger references. That is a more faithful capability analysis than a single benchmark number.aa:T44b,The headline result is on LawBench. An optimized GPT-OSS-20B harness beats a GPT-OSS-120B baseline by 16.05 percentage points at pass@1, but trails it by 4.00 points at pass@64. That is a clean example of improved reliability without superior coverage.

The same pattern appears elsewhere. On HotpotQA and AppWorld, selected harnesses approach or exceed stronger references in aggregate metrics, yet fail to surpass them on hard subsets. The transferred text-classification harness is even more revealing: despite small pass@1 gains on two OOD datasets, it falls below the baseline at pass@64 on all OOD datasets considered. This suggests that optimization can collapse behavior toward safer, more repeatable trajectories, improving first-attempt success while reducing exploratory coverage over multiple attempts.

The main experimental takeaway is that pass@1 and pass@k measure different things and should not be conflated. Harness gains are heterogeneous: they may help easy or medium tasks through better execution stability while hurting hard or OOD tasks by narrowing the search distribution.ab:T5bc,The paper casts collaboration as finite block optimization over x=(x1…xm) with a global loss F(x) accessible via an exact verifier. Each agent b controls block xb and has a cheap local objective Lb that ignores interactions. Define the true conditional change fb(u;x)=F(x with xb←u)-F(x). The key construct is a correction term Rb capturing the interaction effects missing from Lb; agents instead optimize a corrected surrogate \hat{f}_b(u;x)=Lb(u)+\hat{R}_b(u;x), where \hat{R}_b approximates Rb and is anchored so \hat{R}_b(xb;x)=0.
Protocol: (1) parallel private search—each agent proposes an update u_b by optimizing \hat{f}_b with other blocks frozen; (2) exact verification—coordinator evaluates true global deltas via F; (3) compatibility-based merging—build a dependency graph over proposals and select a non-interfering subset (via coloring) to merge, guaranteeing non-increasing F. Extension: even interfering proposals may be merged if the coordinator verifies that their joint application yields a larger decrease; the convergence rate then depends on the realized joint improvement rather than worst-case interference.
Theory: linear convergence up to an explicit error floor determined by correction approximation error; the floor vanishes with exact corrections. whenever unique pretraining data is limited: under repeated exposure to the same tokens, what exactly does random-token replacement improve, and what does it hurt? Prior work mostly reports lower validation loss, but that signal alone cannot separate three different sources of error: approximation error from model class and optimization, estimation error from finite data, and memorization-driven overfitting caused by repeated training on the same corpus. The paper aims to disentangle these effects and to determine whether the benefit of replacement appears at the point of minimum validation loss or only later, after memorization has accumulated and the validation curve starts rising again.","importance":"Its value for pretraining research is not that it introduces a new augmentation, but that it gives a cleaner causal account of why corruption can help in repeated-data regimes. The main contribution is a validation-loss decomposition into approximation, estimation, and memorization terms, enabled by a controlled source with known entropy rate. This leads to a shrinkage interpretation: random-token replacement pulls predictions toward the corpus-average distribution. That view matters because it makes the trade-off explicit. Replacement has an immediate bias cost even before memorization exists, while its benefit only appears once memorization becomes large enough. For practical pretraining, this means the usefulness of corruption depends on stopping time, token budget, and corpus redundancy. That is directly relevant to continual pretraining, domain adaptation on small corpora, synthetic-heavy mixtures, and any setting where models revisit the same data many times.","technical_approach":"$17","experiments":"$18","reading_guide":"$19","authors_note":""},"recommendation":{"zh":"应复现实验里的 loss 分解；它把 repeated-data augmentation 从玄学正则化改成可诊断的 bias-variance 问题。","en":"Reproduce the loss decomposition; it turns repeated-data augmentation from vague regularization into a diagnosable bias-variance problem."},"metadata":{"institutions":["Flitto","Affiliation:Flitto"],"authors":["Wonsup Shin","Jingu Kim"],"notable_authors":[],"tags":["pretraining-data","data-repetition","memorization","input-corruption","validation-loss"],"links":{"arxiv":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27590","pdf":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27590","github":null,"project":null,"source_url":null,"article":null}}},{"id":"2610.27142","title":"ICLHerd: Herding-Based Data Selection for LLMs with In-Context Learning as a Proxy","abstract":"Data selection plays a central role in modern large language model training, as the quality of training data strongly influences downstream performance. In large-scale model training, useful gradient signals can be intermittent across mini-batches, and discarding them on a fixed EMA timescale may be wasteful. At the same time, a long-memory average alone may react too slowly when the parameter region or data mix changes. HyM proposes a compact two-timescale construction: one state accumulates a growing history, while another tracks recent gradients. Because the mechanism is modular, it can be combined with adaptive preconditioners or orthogonalized optimizers such as Muon.","technical_approach":"HyM maintains two momentum states. The slow state m_t is a linearly weighted average over all past gradients; at step t, gradient g_i receives weight 2i/[t(t+1)], so the memory span grows throughout training while assigning larger weight to later gradients. The fast state b_t adds a geometric discount to a similar history, making it behave like conventional EMA momentum after the early phase. The update direction is a linear combination of the scaled slow state and the fast state. The coefficient beta controls the mixing between the two states and also the averaging of iterates. Gradients are evaluated at the training iterate y_t, while the averaged iterate x_t is used for evaluation and checkpointing. The authors also define HyMUON by applying Muon's Newton-Schulz orthogonalization to the combined momentum for matrix-valued parameters. The analysis characterizes cumulative gradient weights and proves an O(T^{-1/2}) expected suboptimality bound for smooth convex objectives at the averaged iterate.","experiments":"The experimental evidence has two parts. The paper also studies how usefulness varies across training examples and how HyM's relative performance changes with batch size. On benchmarks, HyM matches or improves over Schedule-Free on image classification. HyMUON improves over Muon on IWSLT14 and across the evaluated language-modeling settings. For pretrain and post-train researchers, the practical lesson is that verifier quality should be evaluated as a sequential reliability problem, not only as an isolated classification problem.","technical_approach":"The analyzed procedure uses finite local retries. At each step, the model proposes a candidate state, a checker decides whether to accept it, and rejected candidates are retried from the last retained state until the local budget is exhausted. This differs from full-solution sampling, which discards all earlier work, and from broader tree search, which may keep many branches. The analysis gives an attainable trajectory-level reliability bound and an exact accepted-state error threshold for meeting a target reliability under a finite retry cap. The expected-work bound includes paths after incorrect acceptance, which is important because once a bad state is retained, correct-prefix guarantees no longer apply.","experiments":"The experiments use eight reasoning models on composite mathematics and arithmetic tasks. Its real question is: what mechanisms can generate the observed power laws in loss vs. model size, data, and compute, and what exactly do those exponents mean? The paper decomposes scaling into three linked pieces. Geometry explains representation error: how well a finite model can approximate the target function on the data support. Spectral analysis explains data efficiency: how additional samples reveal predictive signal depending on feature visibility, covariance decay, and target alignment. Constrained optimization then turns these error terms into resource-allocation rules under training and inference compute budgets. Standard MoE improves width-wise efficiency by keeping a separate expert pool for each layer and activating only a few experts per token. That helps compute, but it also assumes that experts at different layers should remain topologically independent. The authors question this assumption. If FFN/MoE experts store relatively static knowledge and different layers end up memorizing overlapping content, then layer-private experts may waste parameters through cross-layer duplication. The central question is whether experts can be shared across layers to improve storage efficiency, while keeping the number of activated experts and per-layer compute unchanged, and ideally improving language modeling quality rather than trading it away.","importance":"For pretraining research, the contribution is less about a drop-in MoE tweak and more about opening a different design axis. Most MoE work focuses on routing, load balancing, expert count, or expert specialization within a layer. This paper asks how parameters should be organized across depth. That matters for large-scale pretraining because storage, checkpoint size, and retrieval efficiency become bottlenecks even when FLOPs per token are controlled. The main empirical claim is concrete: with the same number of activated experts and the same expert granularity, a model with Meta Experts reaches performance comparable to vanilla MoE using only about 70% as many experts, while also obtaining lower cross-entropy and better downstream accuracy. In standard speculation, a small model drafts serially and a large model verifies in parallel. ProVe argues that this division is no longer necessary. If the large model already has block-proposal capability, the real bottleneck shifts from drafting to deciding how much of the proposed block can be safely committed. Existing block proposers such as MARS use the proposer’s own confidence to commit a prefix, which is cheap but conservative. The contribution is closer to evaluation and decoding control than to a new pretraining method, but the failure analysis is useful for designing copy-aware data or objectives.","technical_approach":"CopyGen is a lightweight decoding plugin for frozen LMs. It treats copying as a constrained generation problem with three coupled decisions: when copying should start, how far a tentative copied segment should extend, and where copying should stop. During decoding, it measures whether the current output prefix is anchored to the source. Once anchoring is strong enough, it proposes a source span and replays it token by token against the frozen model. The central signal is the logits margin. Positions that should be copied often show a large margin for the correct source token, while mid-span drifts and boundary overruns occur where the margin narrows. A learned bias calibrates these margins during replay, and the decoder emits only the longest prefix that passes the threshold. Unlike pointer-generator models, it does not require architectural changes. Unlike speculative decoding, it is not merely accelerating tokens already accepted by the base model; it adds explicit source-following control.","experiments":"The benchmark covers legal contracts, scientific literature, code contexts, and synthetic random sequences. Across model families and scales, standard decoding makes frequent errors, mainly internal token mismatches and boundary overruns. On three LLM backbones and four task groups, CopyGen improves average exact match by roughly 35 percent relative when applied to frozen models. When combined with supervised fine-tuning, it still adds about 4 percent relative exact-match gain and improves throughput. The random-sequence setting is a useful stress test because it removes much of the semantic support available in natural text.","reading_guide":"Skim in about 20 minutes. The test set has 2,250 human-verified erroneous states over 100 tasks, extracted from 619 failed rollouts by six agents. A tested agent takes over a state 0 to 25 steps after the root cause and is not told that an error occurred. The benchmark reports Error-Awareness Rate, Rubric Score, and Pass@3. The training set contains 8.6K verified recovery trajectories over 377 tasks. The data pipeline, ReRail, converts seed tasks into an executable intermediate representation with a gold lineage that fixes the correct value at every step. It then composes long multi-application workflows over shared persistent state, lets agents execute them via GUI and CLI, keeps verifier-confirmed failures, locates root causes against the gold lineage, and cuts trajectories at controlled depths. For recovery data, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B continues from these cuts with hints of varying specificity, and only verifier-confirmed recoveries are retained.","experiments":"The paper reports several useful empirical facts. In the annotated 619 failures, planning and perception account for 57.3% of root causes, while existing resources such as AgentNet and GUI-Reflection are dominated by execution errors, at 84.3% and 71.2% respectively. Error manifestation is delayed: 78.1% of annotated errors surface at least three steps after the root cause, with a median delay of 17 steps. The scoring interface also matters. On MyPCBench, when the judge reads terminal outputs, tool-call responses, GUI action logs, and screenshots together, GPT-5.5 rises from the officially reported 45.1% Perfect Pass under a screenshot-centric protocol to 85.0% Pass@3. 的集成成本。\n局限也明确：它更像“对某个 solver 定制的对抗式/课程式评测”，跨模型可比性与分布漂移需要额外控制；同时它生成的是评测任务，不直接给出可稳定提升预训练/后训练的训练信号闭环。","technical_approach":"TURTLE 是一个三代理（proposer/solver/feedback generator）的进化式任务生成框架。\n- 任务表示：把 作为进化搜索算子做梯度无关优化。作者强调这允许用闭源强模型当 proposer（只需调用，不需权重/梯度），用进化搜索来迭代产生 mutation。\n- Solver（适配目标模型）：对每个候选变异任务运行 N 次独立尝试，得到经验完成率。\n- Reward/选择准则：核心是“难但可解”，用 completion rate 贴近 50% 的目标来给 proposer 奖励（借鉴 learnability sampling 的直觉：在成功率 0.5 附近方差最大，最能区分能力变化）。这相当于把任务生成变成一个自动课程/自动对抗的折中：避免太易（无信息）与太难（不可诊断）。\n- Feedback generator：基于 solver 的执行轨迹 + ground-truth solution，总结失败原因，作为 proposer 下一轮变异的可利用信号。这里的关键不是“再写一段反思”，而是把反思结构化成可被进化搜索利用的 mutation 方向。\n- 过滤与去伪难：最终用 LLM judge（Gemini 3.6 Flash）过滤掉 trivial failure（格式不匹配、指令歧义、近似复述等）。这一步在 UED 里很关键，否则进化会偏向“卡格式/卡歧义”的捷径。\n- 数据集构建策略：进化跑固定步数后，从每个 parent task 里选 completion rate variance 最高的程序（含并列）进入最终集，意图是保留最能区分 solver 的样本，而不是单纯最难或最易。","experiments":"作者在多个开源 tool-use benchmark 组件上做演示，覆盖 user simulator、检索型文档、47+ SaaS app 模拟、以及更复杂的用户/商品数据库等设置；主 id","starred":false,"priority":"p2","reading_tier":"skim","source":"arxiv","sources":["arxiv"],"published_at":"","category_id":"eval","cover_url":"/covers/2610_27447.png","hf_upvotes":0,"arxiv_categories":["stat.ML","cs.AI","cs.LG","stat.AP","stat.OT"],"summary":{"core_problem":"这篇工作解决的是：在多目标 LLM arena 评测里，如何用尽量少的人类成对比较，可靠识别 strict Pareto frontier 上的模型。传统 arena 往往把不同能力压成一个标量分数，再做单榜单排序；但代码、数学、写作这类能力之间常有明显 trade-off，单一分数会把“某一维很强、另一维一般”的模型过早丢掉。作者把问题形式化为 fixed-confidence sequential identification：每轮只能对一对模型、某一个目标维度拿到一次 Bradley–Terry 偏好反馈，算法需要在给定置信度下停止并输出真实的 strict Pareto frontier。","importance":"对预训练研究本身，它不是训练方法论文，而是评测方法论文；但它切中的问题很现实：当模型能力越来越多维，单一 leaderboard 对模型选择、数据配比、post-train 方向都会产生误导。它的贡献主要有三层。第一，给多目标 arena 一个清晰的统计目标，不再默认“综合分数”就是唯一答案。第二，给出固定置信度、可提前停止的自适应采样算法，适合高成本人评。第三，它把 latent BT score 上的 Pareto 识别，转成可直接从 Bernoulli 比较估计的 vector-Borda 均值问题，这个 reduction 很干净，也让理论分析成立。量级上，这更像评测基础设施层面的改进，而不是会直接改变预训练 recipe 的工作；但如果团队已经在做多维 arena 或内部人评，这篇方法是可以直接借鉴的。","technical_approach":"核心技术是 VB-EGE，Vector-Borda Empirical-Gap Elimination。难点在于：真实目标定义在每个模型的 latent score 向量 θ_i 上，但人评只给出某个目标维度下两模型比较的二元结果，不能直接观测 θ。作者的处理是引入每个维度上的 Borda 坐标：一个模型在该维度对所有对手的平均胜率。对 Bradley–Terry 模型，latent score 越高，和任意对手的胜率越高，因此 Borda 坐标与 latent score 在每个维度上保持同序；于是 strict dominance 和 Pareto frontier 在这个变换下不变。这样，原问题就变成：识别一组 K 个 d 维 Bernoulli 均值向量的 Pareto 集。\n\n在算法层面，VB-EGE 继承了 empirical-gap elimination 的思路，但从单目标扩展到多目标。它维护 active set，只对尚未能判定 Pareto 身份的模型继续采样；一旦有足够统计证据表明某模型被另一模型在所有维度上严格压过，就将其剔除。采样时，比较对象和目标维度不是均匀分配，而是围绕“最难判定的支配关系”集中预算。论文的关键点不只是 elimination，而是如何构造同时覆盖所有模型、所有维度、所有轮次的置信区间，并把这些区间转成 frontier 判定条件。作者还给出 instance-dependent sample complexity 上界，并讨论与信息论下界的关系，说明算法在 gap 依赖上是合理的。这里的 strict Pareto 定义也很重要：作者刻意采用‘每一维都严格更好才算支配’，而不是常见的弱 Pareto。这样做一方面更符合“若某维打平，不应仅凭性能丢弃模型”的决策解释，另一方面避免坐标级 ties 给有限样本终止证明带来的技术麻烦。","experiments":"实验主要验证三件事。第一，真实 arena 数据上是否能更省比较次数地找出 frontier。作者在 Arena-Human-Preference-140K 上，把 code、math、instruction-following 作为三个目标，展示方法能识别出 strict Pareto frontier 上的 3 个模型。第二，和非自适应或更朴素的采样策略相比，VB-EGE 在相同置信要求下需要更少比较，节省主要来自尽早淘汰明显被支配的模型，并把预算集中到 frontier 附近的难例。第三，合成实验里，样本复杂度会随 classification gap denoising pass 中同步预测三种模态。这里的关键不是“多头输出”本身，而是共享主干表示被同时拉向三类预测目标：视频提供局部时空动力学监督，动作提供控制监督，语言提供任务级、较长时程的语义监督。作者强调语言流输出两类文本：下一子任务和 textual memory；这两者在下一控制步会被重新拼回 prompt，形成 language-as-memory loop。与 approa","starred":false,"priority":"p2","reading_tier":"skim","source":"arxiv","sources":["arxiv"],"published_at":"","category_id":"post_train","cover_url":"/covers/2610_27220.png","hf_upvotes":0,"arxiv_categories":["cs.AI"],"summary":{"core_problem":"这篇工作处理的是 的梯度被截断，模型拿不到“前一个软思维选择如何影响后一个思维状态”的训练信号。作者要解决的，就是如何在没有 step-level CoT 标注、只靠最终答案奖励的条件下，既保留 RL 的探索能力，又恢复 soft token 作为可微中间计算的跨步梯度路径，同时避免大词表下软分布过于稠密、语义发散的问题。","importance":"对预训练研究的直接意义，不在于它马上替代标准 next-token 训练，而在于它把“连续中间推理状态”从一个概念性想法推进到更自洽的训练框架。它指出：如果把 soft reasoning 视为 latent computation，而不是离散 action 的替身，那么训练目标和梯度路径都应随之改变。这对几类方向都有启发。第一，RL 与 differentiable latent reasoning 的接口可以怎么设计；第二，reasoning token 是否必须离散化；第三，后训练阶段能否反过来暴露出预训练范式的局限，比如标准 token-level MDP 对内部计算状态的表达能力不足。贡献量级更像方法论上的校正和接口修补，而不是大规模范式替换。对做 pretrain/post-train 闭环的人，这篇比单纯刷分更有参考价值。","technical_approach":"方法核心是 SpaRLax。它有两个关键部件。第一是可微的随机 soft-token 构造。每个 reasoning step，模型先输出词表 logits，再通过 Gumbel reparameterization 引入随机性，得到可采样但仍可反传的 relaxed distribution。和把 Gumbel-softmax 仅当作“近似采样器”的做法不同，这里作者明确利用其可微性，把后续 step 的损失梯度通过当前 soft token 继续往前传，从而恢复 cross-step credit assignment。也就是说，soft token 不再只是 RL 轨迹中的一个黑盒动作，而是序列计算图中的中间节点。\n\n第二是 sparse relaxation。作者观察到，LLM 词表很大，如果直接用 dense softmax 做 embedding mixture，概率质量会摊得很开，很多低概率 token 也会进入加权和，导致 reasoning state 被长尾噪声污染。为此他们在 Gumbel 扰动后不用 softmax，而用 entmax 生成稀疏分布。entmax 的好处是可以给大量低分 token 精确置零，同时保留少数候选的连续混合，因此既保留“superposition”表达能力，又让每一步 reasoning 更聚焦。论文还强调 entmax 的稀疏程度会随不确定性自适应变化，这比手工 top-k 截断更平滑，也更适合端到端训练。\n\n训练框架上，作者把方法放在受控的 GRPO setting 下，与已有 soft-CoT post-training 方法比较。奖励来自最终答案正确性，而不是中间 CoT 监督。推理时既评估 soft-CoT inference，也评估 hard-CoT inference，目的是看训练出的连续 reasoning 能否迁移回标准离散解码。这个设计很重要，因为如果收益只存在于特殊推理器里，方法的通用性会弱很多。","experiments":"实验覆盖 9 个 benchmark，类型包括数学、知识密集推理和代码推理。全文给出的主结论是：在统一 GRPO 框架下，SpaRLax 在加权平均表现上优于对比的 soft-CoT post-training 方法，而且这个优势同时出现在 soft inference 和 hard inference 两种测试方式下。这个结果支持两个判断：一是恢复跨步梯度确实比把 soft token 当不可微 action 更有效；二是训练得到的改进不完全依赖测试时继续使用软思维表示。\n\n作者还做了两类值得注意的分析。第一类是 superposition 使用程度分析。论文声称 SpaRLax 比已有方法更能利用 soft token 中编码的多候选语义，而不是退化成接近 one-hot 的伪离散表示。这个点很关键，因为很多 soft reasoning 方法最后会塌缩成“只是更贵的离散 CoT”。第二类是 sparsity 机制分析。作者比较了不同 candidate-set size 和不同归一化方式，结论是 entmax consistently 优于 dense softmax，说明在大词表场景下，抑制长尾噪声不是细节，而是 soft reasoning 能否成立的必要条件之一。\n\n从你给的全文片段里，没有看到完整的参数量、训练 token 数、各 benchmark 逐项分数和提升幅度表，因此没法负责任地填具体数值。精读时应重点核对实验章节和附录表格，尤其是：基座模型规模、RL rollout 配置、soft reasoning 长度、Gumbel 温度、entmax α 参数、以及 hard/soft inference 的具体解码协议。这些细节会直接影响方法是否可复现，以及收益到底来自训练目标还是来自推理器差异。","reading_guide":"这篇适合泛读到中等深度，不必逐式推导，但有几个点值得认真看。\n\n先看 Introduction 和方法动机。重点不是“soft CoT 能更强”这个常见叙述，而是作者对 RL Prior work still forces them into an RL view by treating soft tokens as sampled actions, but that breaks cross-step gradient flow and loses the signal of how one soft reasoning state shapes the next. The paper formalizes this as a factual access state: a fact is reached not by a single entity key, but by a region of states determined by the visible entity, the surface form of the relation, and the query direction.","importance":"The main contribution is a mechanism-level account of factual recall in diffusion LMs. The paper shows that factual access in DLMs is assembled much earlier than the AR analogy would suggest: layer-0 attention routes relation wording into the visible entity position, and early MLPs read out the fact from this fused state. This has direct consequences for pretraining-oriented analysis. AR knowledge-editing sites do not transfer cleanly to DLMs; edit evaluation must include paraphrases, reverse questions, and masked views; and entity-position states can serve as relation-specific retrieval vectors. The work is useful because it connects a modeling difference of DLMs—bidirectional masked conditionals—to concrete editing and retrieval behavior.","technical_approach":"$8c","experiments":"$8d","reading_guide":"Read Section 2 carefully. The attention-surgery result on relation-to-entity edges is the central mechanism evidence. transformer，在训练目标完全相同、训练长度固定的条件下，为什么会收敛到两类机制上不同的排序算法，而且这两类算法的长度泛化能力差异很大。作者关心的不是“能不能把训练集做对”，而是“模型到底学到了什么算法、这些算法为什么会在更长序列上分化、初始化为什么会把训练推向不同解”。这和预训练里的核心问题是同构的：同样的 loss SEP，模型在 SEP 之后自回归输出升序序列。主实验训练长度固定为 K=16，评测时把 K 从 2 扫到 N。模型是两层、单头、因果 mask 的 transformer，并且去掉位置编码。去位置编码不是为了简化实现，而是为了避免绝对位置成为长度泛化的结构性障碍；作者也提到，加位置编码后模型会学到更难解释、且对已见长度更依赖的位置相关策略。\n\n核心发现是两类解。第一类是“单阶段解”：虽然模型有两层，但第二层注意力几乎不参与排序，做 layer ablation 后性能基本不变。这类解更像一层内完成主要选择逻辑。第二类是“真正两阶段解”：两层都不可缺，去掉第二层会明显掉性能，而且这类解在更长长度上几乎完美泛化。\n\n作者对两阶段解给了两个关键机制解释。其一是 cross-layer specialization。第一层和第二层不是重复做同一件事，而是分工：面对数值彼此接近、gap 很小的相邻元素时，两层协作能更稳定地区分候选项。作者把 gap 定义为排序后相邻元素差值，并指出小 gap 序列在训练长度 K=16 时相对少见，但长度增加后会更常见，因此是否学会处理“小间隔难例”决定了长度泛化。其二是 hinting mechanism。第一层先把“可能的下一个 token 范围”压缩成一个候选集或提示信号，第二层再在这个较小候选空间里做选择。随着输入长度变长，潜在候选数增长，这种先提示、再判别的两阶段结构比单层直接选下一个 token 更稳。\n\n训练动力学上，作者进一步研究为什么会落到哪一类解。他们发现可以通过分层初始化尺度来显著改变收敛结果，也就是用 initialization steering 把模型推向单阶段或两阶段算法。这一点很重要，因为它说明解的分岔不是偶然的后验解释，而是训练早期可控的动力学结果。文中还把类似分析扩展到 minimum-finding 和 greedy coin denomination：minimum-finding 上更简单的一层式解反而泛化更好；coin 任务则出现更多混合解型。这说明“复杂解更泛化”不是普遍规律，而是任务结构、稀有样本统计和层间分工共同决定的。","experiments":"实验设置相当克制，但足够支撑结论。主设定是 K=16 训练，在线采样，batch size 4096，AdamW，学习率 0.03，总训练 60,000 都会影响稀疏度，二者有交互，不是简单归因于模板。4）合成实验中，真正被监督学习到的 target 往往出现单特征 readout，而 control 变量即便可读，也通常需要几十个特征；即便 control 与 target 共享一半底层因子，这个差异仍存在。5）在 8 个 student model 上，参考模型的 k* 能预测监督适配所需标签量，经验关系约为 N* ∝ (k*)^0.65。这个结果很关键，因为它把表征稀疏度和 sample efficiency 直接连起来。6）在 continual learning 场景里，旧分类头失效后，dense probe 仍接近基线，说明遗忘有时先发生在头部失配，而不是线性可读性彻底丢失；重新恢复所需标签少于初次学习。7）在 pruning 下，dense probe 性能会下降，且剪枝前 readout 越宽，通常损失越大；但基于 readout feature 的标签分配或参数保护策略并没有稳定优于基线，说明 k* 适合做诊断，不等于已经足够指导干预。","reading_guide":"如果只花一小时，建议先看引言、k* 定义图、base model 主结果图、instruction tuning 对比图、合成控制实验图，以及 continual learning / pruning
